UWSA1:Q001.boardCall: RA patient + acute monoarthritis + fever -> Gram-positive bacterial infection
UWSA1:Q001.hinge: Acute monoarticular inflammation with fever in a pre-existing abnormal joint is septic arthritis until proven otherwise.
UWSA1:Q001.trap: History of rheumatoid arthritis and baseline joint deformities suggest a flare, but acute monoarthritis with fever is septic arthritis.

A.clue: Polyarticular symmetric joint inflammation
A.fit: Not here: acute monoarthritis with fever 38.2 C

B.clue: Pseudomonas or Enterobacteriaceae joint infection
B.fit: Not here: no immunosuppressed neutropenia or central line

C.clue: Staphylococcus aureus monoarticular infection
C.fit: Here: one-day right second MCP pain, 38.2 C, exquisite tenderness

D.clue: Chronic indolent mycobacterial synovitis
D.fit: Not here: one-day acute onset and fever 38.2 C

E.clue: Noninflammatory weight-bearing joint degradation
E.fit: Not here: fever 38.2 C and exquisite MCP tenderness

nodes.text: Acute monoarthritis: arthrocentesis before starting empiric antibiotics
Synovial fluid analysis: cell count, Gram stain, culture, crystals
**WBC > 50,000/mm3 or positive Gram stain:** septic arthritis
**Gram-positive cocci (Staphylococcus aureus):** IV vancomycin + joint drainage
**Crystals present with negative Gram stain:** crystal-induced arthropathy
Serial joint drainage via needle aspiration or arthroscopy
Tailor intravenous antibiotic regimen to synovial culture results

UWSA1:Q002.boardCall: Epigastric pain + AST>ALT + restlessness + tachycardia + hand tremor -> Benzodiazepines
UWSA1:Q002.hinge: Sympathetic hyperactivity 12-24 hours after admission indicates acute alcohol withdrawal.
UWSA1:Q002.trap: The positive urine opiate screen tempts buprenorphine or naloxone, but the clinical picture is alcohol withdrawal.

A.fit: Not here: acute withdrawal with autonomic hyperactivity

B.clue: GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulators
B.fit: Here: tremulous hands, HR 120/min, BP 162/94 mm Hg

C.clue: Partial mu-opioid agonist
C.fit: Not here: autonomic hyperactivity is from alcohol withdrawal

D.clue: Osmotic laxative acidifying colon ammonia
D.fit: Not here: restlessness is withdrawal, no asterixis

E.clue: Pure mu-opioid receptor antagonist
E.fit: Not here: patient is agitated, not in respiratory depression

F.clue: Mu-opioid receptor antagonist for cravings
F.fit: Not here: acute tremor and tachycardia require immediate sedation

nodes.text: Recognize withdrawal: tremor, diaphoresis, insomnia, tachycardia within 6-48 hours
Symptom-triggered intravenous benzodiazepine (lorazepam, diazepam, or chlordiazepoxide)
**Liver failure or elderly:** lorazepam, oxazepam, or temazepam (LOT)
Thiamine + folate + dextrose fluids to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy
Monitor CIWA score in intensive care setting
**Refractory severe agitation:** add phenobarbital or propofol
Transition to oral naltrexone or acamprosate once detoxified

UWSA1:Q003.boardCall: Elderly patient + painless lymphadenopathy + lymphocytosis > 30,000 -> Smudge cells
UWSA1:Q003.hinge: Dramatic asymptomatic mature lymphocytosis with diffuse lymphadenopathy in an older adult indicates CLL, which features fragile smudge cells on smear.
UWSA1:Q003.trap: Cough with green sputum suggests an acute infectious process, but the profound lymphocytosis and smudge cells define CLL.

A.clue: Neutrophils with six or more nuclear lobes
A.fit: Not here: MCV is 89 µm3 and marked lymphocytosis

B.clue: Immature lymphoid precursors with high N:C ratio
B.fit: Not here: mature small lymphocytosis of 92%

C.clue: Azurophilic needle-like inclusions in myeloblasts
C.fit: Not here: leukocytosis consists of 92% lymphocytes

D.clue: Stacks of red blood cells resembling coins
D.fit: Not here: isolated mature leukocytosis without hypercalcemia
D.tempting: elderly man with anemia and lymphadenopathy

E.clue: Fragile mature lymphocytes disrupted during smear preparation
E.fit: Here: leukocytes 38,800/mm3, lymphocytes 92%, nontender lymphadenopathy

F.clue: Dacrocytes from marrow fibrosis or extramedullary hematopoiesis
F.fit: Not here: spleen tip only slightly prominent, marked lymphocytosis

nodes.text: Unexplained absolute lymphocytosis (> 5,000/mm3) with smudge cells on smear
Flow cytometry of peripheral blood: CD19+, CD20+, CD5+, CD23+ B cells
Staging with Rai system: lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, anemia, or thrombocytopenia
**Asymptomatic early stage (Rai 0-II):** active surveillance without immediate chemotherapy
**Advanced stage (Rai III-IV) or bulky disease:** targeted therapy (ibrutinib or venetoclax)
Infection prophylaxis: pneumococcal and influenza vaccines, avoid live vaccines

UWSA1:Q004.boardCall: Postoperative day 3 + confusion + hypotension + leukocytosis -> Blood cultures and antibiotics
UWSA1:Q004.hinge: Acute confusion, tachycardia, hypotension, and leukocytosis in a postoperative patient with an indwelling central line signal sepsis requiring immediate blood cultures and broad-spectrum antibiotics.
UWSA1:Q004.trap: Recent blood transfusion tempts Coombs testing for hemolytic transfusion reaction, but the high leukocytosis and shock point to sepsis.

A.clue: First-line workup and therapy for systemic sepsis
A.fit: Here: confusion, BP 90/50 mm Hg, HR 110/min, WBC 21,000/mm3

B.clue: Direct antiglobulin test for hemolytic transfusion reaction
B.fit: Not here: transfused 2 days ago, hypotension with leukocytosis 21,000/mm3
B.tempting: received 2 units packed red cells postoperatively

C.clue: Anti-inflammatory agents for adrenal insufficiency or ARDS
C.fit: Not here: hemodynamic instability is septic shock, not adrenal insufficiency
C.tempting: hypotension and confusion after major surgery

D.clue: Contrast imaging to detect pulmonary arterial thrombus
D.fit: Not here: normal O2 saturation 96%, lung crackles cleared with cough

E.clue: Neuroimaging for acute intracerebral infarction or hemorrhage
E.fit: Not here: nonfocal neurologic exam, hypotension and fever indicate sepsis

F.clue: Emergent surgical re-exploration of abdominal cavity
F.fit: Not here: soft abdomen, normal bowel sounds, clean wound drainage

nodes.text: Recognize postoperative sepsis: confusion, BP 90/50 mm Hg, HR 110/min, WBC 21,000/mm3
Draw peripheral and central line blood cultures, then start IV vancomycin + cefepime
Intravenous crystalloid bolus for septic shock
**Persistent hypotension despite fluids:** start norepinephrine infusion
Inspect central line insertion site and remove catheter if infection suspected
Investigate secondary sources: urinalysis, chest x-ray, abdominal CT if peritoneal signs

UWSA1:Q005.boardCall: Parenteral nutrition via central line -> Bloodstream infection
UWSA1:Q005.hinge: Central venous catheterization for parenteral nutrition carries central line-associated bloodstream infection as its most frequent and serious complication.
UWSA1:Q005.trap: Nutritional therapy initiation tempts refeeding syndrome, but that occurs in severely malnourished patients, whereas this patient had a normal BMI.

A.clue: Central venous catheter-related bacteremia or fungemia
A.fit: Here: parenteral nutrition started through a central venous catheter

B.clue: Gallbladder sludge and stone formation from biliary stasis
B.fit: Not here: develops after weeks of parenteral nutrition, not acutely

C.clue: Hypervolemia from excessive parenteral infusion volume
C.fit: Not here: normal cardiac and renal function, BMI 26 kg/m2

D.clue: Low blood glucose from abrupt parenteral nutrition cessation
D.fit: Not here: occurs upon abrupt cessation, hyperglycemia is more common

E.clue: Severe hypophosphatemia upon feeding chronically starved patient
E.fit: Not here: previously healthy man with normal baseline BMI 26 kg/m2

nodes.text: Central venous catheter for parenteral nutrition carries high risk of bloodstream infection
Bloodstream infection prevention: sterile insertion technique, chlorhexidine dressing, prompt line removal
Monitor daily blood glucose, serum electrolytes, liver enzymes, and catheter site
**Fever or catheter site erythema:** draw blood cultures + start empiric vancomycin + cefepime
**Persistent fungemia or bacteremia:** remove central venous catheter
Transition to enteral nutrition as bowel function recovers

UWSA1:Q006.boardCall: Acutely psychotic patient + violent behavior + fleeing -> Physically restrain and administer intramuscular antipsychotic
UWSA1:Q006.hinge: An acutely psychotic patient who poses an immediate physical danger to staff cannot be allowed to leave and requires emergency physical restraint with chemical sedation.
UWSA1:Q006.trap: Respecting patient autonomy tempts letting him leave, but acute psychosis with danger to self/others negates decision-making capacity.

A.clue: Involuntary discharge of incapacitated agitated patient
A.fit: Not here: patient is agitated, psychotic, and dangerous
A.tempting: respecting autonomy and patient request to leave

B.clue: Mechanical immobilization without chemical sedation
B.fit: Not here: chemical sedation is required to prevent self-harm
B.tempting: desire to avoid sedating before examination

C.clue: De-escalation by family or peers
C.fit: Not here: violent physical assault requires immediate containment
C.tempting: roommates brought patient and might calm him

D.clue: Seclusion without pharmacologic intervention
D.fit: Not here: acute violent struggle requires immediate medication
D.tempting: separates patient from others in department

E.clue: Rapid tranquilization plus physical containment
E.fit: Here: acute severe agitation, paranoia, physical assault, and fleeing

algorithm.title: Acute psychotic agitation in emergency department

nodes.text: Recognize acute agitation and danger to self or others: attempt verbal de-escalation
**Verbal de-escalation fails with violent behavior:** physically restrain patient and administer intramuscular antipsychotic
Choose rapid-acting intramuscular haloperidol, ziprasidone, or olanzapine
**Severe agitation refractory to antipsychotic:** add intramuscular lorazepam
Continuous close monitoring: vital signs, pulse oximetry, airway, restraint checks every 15 minutes
Perform medical workup once calmed: glucose, toxicology, electrolytes, head imaging if indicated

UWSA1:Q007.boardCall: Severe agitation + prolonged QTc 505 ms -> Lorazepam
UWSA1:Q007.hinge: When QTc is prolonged (> 500 ms), antipsychotics are contraindicated due to torsades risk; benzodiazepines like lorazepam provide safe sedation.
UWSA1:Q007.trap: Prior improvement with ziprasidone tempts giving another dose, but the prolonged QTc of 505 ms forbids further antipsychotics.

A.clue: Second-generation antipsychotic with high QTc risk
A.fit: Not here: QTc interval is 505 ms

B.clue: First-generation antipsychotic prolonging cardiac repolarization
B.fit: Not here: prolonged QTc of 505 ms increases torsades risk

C.clue: Mood stabilizer with slow onset of action
C.fit: Not here: takes days to achieve therapeutic effect
C.tempting: patient shows manic features and paranoia

D.clue: Short-acting benzodiazepine without cardiac repolarization effects
D.fit: Here: recurrent agitation, kicking, shouting, and QTc 505 ms

E.clue: Mechanical immobilization without chemical sedation
E.fit: Not here: acute violent kicking requires safe chemical sedation
E.tempting: avoids adding drugs that prolong QTc

nodes.text: Recognize severe agitation with prolonged QTc interval (> 500 ms)
Avoid additional antipsychotics: high risk of torsades de pointes and ventricular arrhythmia
Administer intramuscular lorazepam for rapid chemical sedation
**Persistent extreme violent behavior:** repeat lorazepam dose + monitor airway and telemetry
Correct underlying electrolyte abnormalities: check potassium, magnesium, and calcium
Obtain serial ECGs until QTc normalizes below 450 ms

UWSA1:Q008.boardCall: Toddler + painless large maroon stools + normal exam -> Ectopic gastric mucosa
UWSA1:Q008.hinge: Painless, large-volume maroon rectal bleeding in an otherwise well toddler is the classic presentation of Meckel diverticulum containing ectopic gastric mucosa.
UWSA1:Q008.trap: Currant jelly stools of intussusception are tempting, but intussusception features severe colicky abdominal pain, fussiness, and vomiting.

A.clue: Neoplastic colonic mucosal projection
A.fit: Not here: presents with painless hematochezia streaks, not large maroon stools
A.tempting: causes lower GI bleeding in young children

B.clue: Heterotopic acid-secreting tissue ulcerating adjacent ileal mucosa
B.fit: Here: 18-month-old passing large maroon stools with soft nontender abdomen

C.clue: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposition
C.fit: Not here: no palpable purpura, arthritis, or colicky abdominal pain
C.tempting: causes lower gastrointestinal bleeding in toddlers

D.clue: Chronic transmural or mucosal intestinal inflammation
D.fit: Not here: acute presentation without chronic diarrhea, fever, or weight loss

E.clue: Invagination of bowel segment into downstream lumen
E.fit: Not here: painless bleeding, abdomen soft and nontender, child not fussy
E.tempting: common cause of maroon stools in toddlers

algorithm.title: Painless lower gastrointestinal bleeding in toddler

nodes.text: Painless maroon stools in child under 2 years: suspect Meckel diverticulum
Ectopic gastric mucosa in vitelline duct remnant secretes acid causing ileal ulceration
Diagnostic workup: technetium-99m pertechnetate scintigraphy (Meckel scan)
**Active brisk hemorrhage:** mesenteric angiography or emergent exploratory laparotomy
Definitive management: surgical resection of diverticulum or segmental ileal excision
Correct anemia and hypovolemia with isotonic intravenous fluids or blood transfusion

UWSA1:Q009.boardCall: Fever + hypotension 70/60 + pH 7.24 + PaCO2 30 -> Increased tissue metabolic acid production
UWSA1:Q009.hinge: Septic shock produces systemic tissue hypoperfusion and anaerobic glycolysis, resulting in increased lactic acid production and high anion gap metabolic acidosis.
UWSA1:Q009.trap: A history of diabetes tempts ketoacidosis, but the blood glucose of 154 mg/dL excludes DKA as the primary cause.

A.clue: V/Q imbalance causing hypoxemia and respiratory alkalosis
A.fit: Not here: PaO2 is 85 mm Hg and pH 7.24 indicates acidemia

B.clue: Proximal renal tubular acidosis type 2 defect
B.fit: Not here: acute septic shock with warm extremities, not chronic RTA
B.tempting: metabolic acidosis can stem from renal loss

C.clue: Excessive secretory chloride loss with alkalosis
C.fit: Not here: vomiting causes metabolic alkalosis, not acidemia pH 7.24
C.tempting: patient had an episode of vomiting

D.clue: Accelerated ketogenesis causing diabetic ketoacidosis
D.fit: Not here: fingerstick blood glucose is only 154 mg/dL

E.clue: Anaerobic glycolysis generating lactic acid during hypoperfusion
E.fit: Here: pH 7.24, PaCO2 30 mm Hg, BP 70/60 mm Hg, T 38.9 C

nodes.text: Recognize septic shock: fever 38.9 C, BP 70/60 mm Hg, warm extremities, bronchial breath sounds
Hypoperfusion drives anaerobic glycolysis: increased tissue metabolic acid production
Immediate resuscitation: intravenous crystalloid bolus + broad-spectrum antibiotics
**Refractory hypotension after fluids:** start norepinephrine infusion to target MAP ≥ 65 mm Hg
Draw blood cultures + check serum lactate and arterial blood gases
Identify source: chest x-ray for aspiration pneumonia, initiate pulmonary hygiene

UWSA1:Q010.boardCall: Metastatic cancer + anemia + thrombocytopenia + INR 3.2 + low fibrinogen -> Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia
UWSA1:Q010.hinge: Consumptive coagulopathy and brisk hemolysis reflect DIC causing microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.
UWSA1:Q010.trap: Known lytic bone metastases tempt bone marrow infiltration, but the acute onset with severe coagulopathy confirms DIC and microangiopathic hemolysis.

A.clue: Myelophthisic anemia with leukoerythroblastic smear and dacrocytes
A.fit: Not here: acute 3-day drop from normal CBC with coagulopathy

B.clue: Hepcidin-mediated iron trapping with low reticulocyte count
B.fit: Not here: reticulocyte count is 7.6% and LDH is 1200 U/L

C.clue: Autoantibody-mediated erythrocyte destruction with normal coagulation
C.fit: Not here: elevated INR 3.2 and low fibrinogen 125 mg/dL indicate DIC
C.tempting: hemolytic labs with high reticulocytes and indirect bilirubin

D.clue: Mechanical erythrocyte shearing by microvascular fibrin thrombi
D.fit: Here: reticulocytes 7.6%, platelets 42,000/mm3, INR 3.2, fibrinogen 125 mg/dL

E.clue: Microcytic hypochromic anemia with low ferritin and reticulocytopenia
E.fit: Not here: normal MCV 85 fl and reticulocytes 7.6%
E.tempting: fatigue and weakness in female cancer patient

F.clue: Macrocytic megaloblastic anemia from defective thymidylate synthesis
F.fit: Not here: normal MCV 85 fl and acute drop in platelets

nodes.text: Recognize DIC: acute thrombocytopenia, elevated INR, low fibrinogen, elevated LDH, reticulocytosis
Peripheral blood smear: schistocytes confirming microangiopathic hemolytic anemia
Treat underlying malignancy or precipitating systemic infection
**Active bleeding or high procedure risk with platelets < 50,000/mm3:** transfuse platelets
**Hypofibrinogenemia (< 150 mg/dL) with active hemorrhage:** infuse cryoprecipitate
**Prolonged INR with active hemorrhage:** administer fresh frozen plasma
Avoid antifibrinolytic agents (tranexamic acid) due to risk of fatal thrombosis

UWSA1:Q091.hinge: Procedural pleural puncture during subclavian or axillary venous access creates a one-way air leak with tension physiology.

A.tempting: heavy smoking history with underlying COPD

B.clue: Chemical lung inflammation after witnessed macroaspiration
B.fit: Not here: acute post-procedural dyspnea without witnessed vomiting or aspiration

D.fit: Not here: chest radiograph shows distinct visceral pleural line without vascular congestion
D.tempting: underlying ischemic cardiomyopathy with low ejection fraction

E.clue: Fluid accumulation in the pleural space with blunting
E.fit: Not here: imaging demonstrates air in the pleural cavity rather than fluid layering
E.tempting: postoperative shortness of breath and dullness

F.clue: Sudden pulmonary arterial occlusion with right heart strain
F.fit: Not here: visible visceral pleural line and hyperlucency on chest radiograph
F.tempting: sudden postoperative dyspnea and sinus tachycardia

G.fit: Here: sudden worsening dyspnea, hypoxia on 10 L, following ICD implantation

nodes.text: Recognize acute dyspnea and tachycardia immediately following central venous or cardiac device instrumentation
**Hemodynamic instability (severe hypotension, tracheal deviation):** immediate emergent needle thoracostomy
**Hemodynamically stable:** obtain urgent portable chest radiograph to identify visceral pleural line and mediastinal shift
Insert chest tube (tube thoracostomy) into pleural space connected to water-seal drainage system
Administer supplemental high-flow oxygen to accelerate pleural nitrogen reabsorption
Monitor serial chest radiographs until complete lung re-expansion and resolution of air leak

UWSA1:Q092.boardCall: Obese woman with PCOS and anovulatory infertility -> Weight loss (first-line intervention to restore ovulation).
UWSA1:Q092.hinge: Lifestyle modification with weight loss decreases peripheral estrone conversion, lowering circulating insulin and restoring spontaneous ovulation.
UWSA1:Q092.trap: Letrozole or clomiphene can induce ovulation, but weight loss is the essential first-line intervention for obese patients.

A.clue: Dopamine D2 agonist for hyperprolactinemic anovulation
A.fit: Not here: completely normal serum prolactin level rules out hyperprolactinemia

B.clue: Cyclic hormones for endometrial protection and cycle control
B.fit: Not here: patient is actively seeking conception; combined hormones prevent pregnancy

C.clue: Surgical resection of intrauterine synechiae
C.fit: Not here: normal pelvic examination without history of uterine curettage or infection

D.clue: Assisted reproduction depositing washed sperm into uterus
D.fit: Not here: partner semen analysis is normal and anovulation has not been addressed

E.clue: Aldosterone and androgen receptor antagonist
E.fit: Not here: spironolactone is teratogenic (feminizes male fetus) and contraindicated in conception

F.clue: Flushing fallopian tubes with oil-based contrast
F.fit: Not here: primary etiology is anovulation secondary to PCOS rather than tubal occlusion

G.clue: Lifestyle weight reduction restoring spontaneous ovulatory cycles
G.fit: Here: 26-year-old with BMI 33, oligomenorrhea, hirsutism, seeking conception

nodes.text: Confirm anovulatory infertility in PCOS: oligomenorrhea, hyperandrogenism, and metabolic obesity
Prescribe structured lifestyle modification and weight loss as the first-line intervention
**Persistent anovulation despite weight reduction:** initiate ovulation induction with oral letrozole (aromatase inhibitor)
**Second-line ovulation induction:** administer clomiphene citrate or exogenous gonadotropin injections
**Patients not desiring immediate pregnancy:** prescribe combined oral contraceptive pills for cycle regulation and hirsutism
Screen all PCOS patients for metabolic comorbidities: 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test and lipid profile

UWSA1:Q093.boardCall: Recurrent brief (< 1 min) vertigo episodes triggered by head movements -> Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo -> canalith repositioning (Epley maneuver).
UWSA1:Q093.hinge: Brief spinning sensation lasting under 1 minute triggered by dynamic head movements without hearing loss or tinnitus.
UWSA1:Q093.trap: History of migraines might suggest vestibular migraine, but discrete seconds-long positional spells fit BPPV.

A.clue: Secondary prevention for posterior circulation stroke
A.fit: Not here: brief self-resolving positional vertigo with normal focal neurological examination

B.clue: Maintenance therapy for endolymphatic hydrops
B.fit: Not here: normal hearing examination and lack of episodic tinnitus or aural fullness

C.clue: Prophylactic daily pharmacotherapy for vestibular migraine
C.fit: Not here: vertigo episodes last seconds rather than hours and are provoked by head position

D.clue: Canalith repositioning clearing semicircular canal debris
D.fit: Here: episodic intense spinning lasting under a minute provoked by head position changes

E.clue: Anti-inflammatory therapy for acute vestibular neuritis
E.fit: Not here: brief episodic vertigo triggered by position rather than days of continuous vertigo

nodes.text: Evaluate episodic vertigo lasting < 1 minute provoked by head position changes without auditory deficits
Perform Dix-Hallpike maneuver to elicit transient torsional upbeating nystagmus and vertigo
Treat definitively with canalith repositioning maneuvers (Epley maneuver) to return otoliths to utricle
**Refractory or atypical nystagmus (downbeating, non-fatiguing):** perform contrast brain MRI to rule out posterior fossa lesion
**Meniere disease (episodic vertigo + sensorineural hearing loss + tinnitus):** restrict sodium and caffeine + initiate thiazide diuretic
Reassure patient regarding benign nature and demonstrate home Brandt-Daroff exercises if positional dizziness recurs

UWSA1:Q094.boardCall: Ulnar neuropathy + numbness of 4th/5th digits AND medial dorsum of hand + worse with elbow flexion -> Cubital tunnel compression at elbow.
UWSA1:Q094.hinge: Sensory loss involving the medial dorsum of the hand (dorsal cutaneous branch) and hypothenar eminence localizes compression to the elbow rather than the wrist.
UWSA1:Q094.trap: Guyon canal compression at the wrist spares the dorsal cutaneous branch, which branches proximal to the wrist.

A.clue: C8 radiculopathy with neck pain and dermatomal loss
A.fit: Not here: lack of neck pain or dermatomal sensory loss extending into medial forearm
A.tempting: numbness involving fourth and fifth fingers

B.clue: Lower trunk brachial plexopathy from thoracic outlet
B.fit: Not here: weakness isolated to ulnar territory without median nerve thenar involvement

C.clue: Ulnar nerve compression at cubital tunnel
C.fit: Here: paresthesias in 4th/5th digits, hypothenar eminence, medial hand dorsum, worse on phone

D.clue: Anterior interosseous nerve syndrome in forearm
D.fit: Not here: sensory loss in ulnar territory; anterior interosseous nerve has no cutaneous sensory innervation

E.clue: Ulnar nerve entrapment at Guyon canal
E.fit: Not here: compression at wrist spares the dorsal cutaneous and hypothenar sensory branches
E.tempting: decreased sensation in fourth and fifth fingers

nodes.text: Perform targeted sensory examination of the hand: compare palmar digits against hypothenar and dorsal hand surfaces
**Sensory deficit over dorsal cutaneous and hypothenar regions:** localizes compression to the elbow (cubital tunnel)
**Sensory deficit restricted to palmar digits with intact dorsal sensation:** localizes compression to the wrist (Guyon canal)
Obtain electromyography and nerve conduction studies to confirm focal slowing across the elbow
Conservative management: avoid sustained elbow flexion, apply nocturnal elbow splint in extension, and ergonomic pad
**Progressive motor weakness or persistent sensory loss despite splinting:** surgical decompression or anterior transposition

UWSA1:Q095.boardCall: Mixed upper motor neuron (hyperreflexia, extensor plantar) + lower motor neuron (atrophy, fasciculations) deficits without sensory loss -> Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
UWSA1:Q095.hinge: Progressive combination of lower motor neuron atrophy and upper motor neuron hyperreflexia/Babinski sign with completely intact sensory pathways.
UWSA1:Q095.trap: Hand atrophy with mild CK elevation might mimic myopathy or neuropathy, but prominent upper motor neuron signs (Babinski, hyperreflexia) rule out isolated peripheral disorders.

B.clue: Peripheral nerve demyelination with diffuse hyporeflexia
B.fit: Not here: brisk hyperactive knee jerk and positive extensor plantar (Babinski) response

C.clue: Proximal myopathy with markedly elevated CK
C.fit: Not here: prominent distal hand atrophy and upper motor neuron signs with mild CK 450
C.tempting: feeling weak with elevated creatine kinase

D.clue: CNS demyelinating lesions separated in time/space

D.tempting: upper motor neuron signs and gait instability

E.clue: Genetic progressive muscle wasting with severe CK elevation

E.tempting: hand muscle atrophy and gait imbalance

F.fit: Not here: bilateral hand muscle atrophy (cervical level) without sensory deficit or sphincter changes

**Papillary muscle rupture (apical holosystolic murmur + tall v waves on PCWP tracing):** emergent mitral valve replacement
**Free wall rupture (pericardial tamponade + electromechanical dissociation):** emergent pericardiocentesis and surgical patch repair

nodes.text: Analyze 12-lead ECG: relationship between P waves, PR interval duration, and QRS conduction

**Mobitz type II second-degree AV block (constant PR, unpredictable dropped QRS):** high risk of complete block; place permanent pacemaker
**Third-degree complete AV block (complete AV dissociation):** emergent temporary transvenous pacing followed by permanent pacemaker

algorithm.title: Peripheral artery disease and ischemic ulceration

Medical therapy: prescribe high-intensity statin, aspirin, blood pressure control, and structured supervised exercise
**Chronic limb-threatening ischemia (rest pain, nonhealing gangrene/ulcers):** perform urgent revascularization (endovascular or surgical bypass)

G.fit: Not here: estrogen stimulates hepatic procoagulant factor synthesis, increasing venous thromboembolism risk 2- to 4-fold

algorithm.title: Benefits and risks of combined oral contraceptives

nodes.text: Review patient history, cardiovascular risk factors, and cancer family history prior to prescribing combined hormonal contraceptives
Document proven cancer protective benefits: sustained reduction in epithelial ovarian cancer and endometrial adenocarcinoma risk
Mechanism of ovarian cancer protection: suppression of ovulation reduces repetitive follicular rupture and ovarian surface epithelial trauma
Prescribe combined oral contraceptive pills (ethinyl estradiol + progestin) for pregnancy prevention and menstrual cycle regulation
**Uncontrolled hypertension or smoking age ≥ 35:** select progestin-only pills or levonorgestrel intrauterine device
Counsel on potential risks: modest increased risk of venous thromboembolism and cervical dysplasia during active use

UWSA1:Q136.boardCall: Septic shock (warm extremity, bounding pulses, low BP, high lactate) -> low PCWP + high cardiac index + low SVR + high mixed venous O2 (↓ | ↑ | ↓ | ↑).
UWSA1:Q136.hinge: Peripheral arteriolar vasodilation reduces systemic vascular resistance, stimulating high compensatory cardiac output and elevated mixed venous oxygen saturation.
UWSA1:Q136.trap: Late or cold septic shock can show low cardiac output, but acute warm septic shock demonstrates high cardiac index and low SVR.

A.clue: Cardiogenic shock with elevated PCWP and low CI
A.fit: Not here: warm extremity with bounding pulses indicates hyperdynamic distributive shock rather than cardiogenic pump failure

B.clue: Hypovolemic shock with low preload and high SVR
B.fit: Not here: warm extremities and bounding pulses indicate distributive shock

C.clue: Low PCWP, low cardiac index, and elevated SVR
C.fit: Not here: systemic vascular resistance is markedly reduced in septic distributive shock due to inflammatory vasodilation

D.clue: Distributive septic shock with hyperdynamic cardiac output
D.fit: Here: cellulitis, BP 80/52, bounding pulses, warm extremities, elevated lactate, leukocytosis 18,000

E.clue: High preload, high output, low SVR
E.fit: Not here: venodilation and capillary leak in sepsis decrease central venous and pulmonary capillary wedge pressures

F.clue: Elevated biventricular filling with depressed SVR and SvO2
F.fit: Not here: warm extremities reflect hyperdynamic state with increased mixed venous oxygen

nodes.text: Identify distributive (septic) shock: profound hypotension (MAP < 65 mm Hg), tachycardia, warm extremities, and bounding pulses
Hemodynamic profile: decreased preload (low PCWP), elevated cardiac index (hyperdynamic LV output), and markedly decreased SVR
Mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) is elevated due to rapid capillary transit and impaired peripheral cellular extraction
Initiate rapid intravenous volume resuscitation with isotonic crystalloids within 3 hours
**Persistent hypotension (MAP < 65 mm Hg) despite fluids:** administer intravenous norepinephrine infusion as first-line vasopressor
Administer empiric broad-spectrum intravenous antimicrobials within 1 hour of septic shock recognition

UWSA1:Q137.boardCall: Painful nonhealing cutaneous ulcer + hearing loss/otitis + nephritic sediment (RBCs, proteinuria) -> Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Necrotizing vasculitis).
UWSA1:Q137.hinge: Upper respiratory tract involvement (hearing loss, otitis), glomerulonephritis, and cutaneous ulceration (pyoderma gangrenosum-like or leukocytoclastic vasculitis) indicate systemic necrotizing vasculitis.
UWSA1:Q137.trap: Nonhealing leg ulcer tempts toward peripheral artery disease or bacterial ecthyma, but multisystem disease with nephritis and otalgia proves vasculitis.

A.clue: Ecthyma gangrenosum or chronic pyogenic skin ulceration
A.fit: Not here: multisystem disease with recent otitis, hearing loss, and active glomerulonephritis confirms systemic vasculitis

B.clue: Sickle cell disease causing microvascular cutaneous ulceration
B.fit: Not here: lack of chronic hemolytic anemia and presence of active glomerulonephritis and otitis

C.clue: Opportunistic cutaneous ulceration in impaired cellular immunity
C.fit: Not here: normal leukocyte count and robust inflammatory necrotizing vasculitis involving ear and kidneys

D.clue: Hypoalbuminemia and zinc deficiency impairing wound healing
D.fit: Not here: acute febrile multisystem illness with hearing loss, elevated creatinine, and nephritic urine sediment

E.clue: Small-to-medium vessel necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis
E.fit: Here: painful leg ulcer, fever, hearing loss, and hematuria with casts

F.clue: Atherosclerotic arterial insufficiency with ischemic ulcer
F.fit: Not here: acute painful nodule with nephritic sediment and otitis

nodes.text: Identify multisystem small-to-medium vessel vasculitis: otitis/sinusitis, pulmonary infiltrates, and glomerulonephritis
Diagnostic serology: check antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (c-ANCA directed against proteinase-3 [PR3])
Obtain tissue biopsy (nasal, skin ulcer, lung, or kidney) demonstrating necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis and pauci-immune crescentic GN
Remission induction: administer high-dose systemic corticosteroids (methylprednisolone) + cyclophosphamide or rituximab
**Severe alveolar hemorrhage or rapidly progressive renal failure:** perform adjunctive plasma exchange (plasmapheresis)
**Remission achieved:** transition to maintenance therapy with azathioprine or methotrexate

UWSA1:Q138.boardCall: Heavy smoker + severe acute hypercalcemia (> 14 mg/dL) + progressive lethargy -> Hypercalcemia of malignancy (PTHrP secretion or osteolytic metastases).
UWSA1:Q138.hinge: Marked severe hypercalcemia (> 14 mg/dL) with rapid clinical onset and lethargy in an elderly smoker is characteristic of malignancy rather than primary hyperparathyroidism.
UWSA1:Q138.trap: Primary hyperparathyroidism causes mild chronic asymptomatic hypercalcemia (< 12 mg/dL), whereas severe symptomatic hypercalcemia (> 14 mg/dL) indicates malignancy.

A.clue: Adrenal cortical insufficiency with hyperkalemia and hyponatremia
A.fit: Not here: sodium is 142 mEq/L and potassium is 4.4 mEq/L

B.clue: Thyrotoxic osteoclast activation with suppressed TSH
B.fit: Not here: produces mild hypercalcemia (< 11 mg/dL); severe hypercalcemia > 14 mg/dL indicates malignancy

C.clue: Tumor-mediated osteolysis or systemic PTHrP secretion
C.fit: Here: 72-year-old smoker with progressive lethargy, back pain, and severe calcium 14.1 mg/dL

D.clue: Disorganized bone remodeling with isolated high alkaline phosphatase
D.fit: Not here: Paget disease typically presents with normal serum calcium and markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase

E.clue: Autonomous parathyroid adenoma secreting authentic PTH
E.fit: Not here: causes mild chronic hypercalcemia, not severe elevation 14.1 mg/dL

F.clue: Reduced urinary calcium clearance from distal tubule thiazides
F.fit: Not here: thiazides produce mild hypercalcemia, not severe elevation 14.1 mg/dL

nodes.text: Recognize severe hypercalcemia (serum calcium > 14 mg/dL): lethargy, delirium, constipation, polyuria, and dehydration
Initial resuscitation: administer aggressive intravenous isotonic saline hydration (200-300 mL/hr) to restore intravascular volume
Concurrent medical therapy: administer subcutaneous calcitonin for rapid transient lowering of calcium within 12-24 hours
Administer intravenous bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid or pamidronate) for sustained inhibition of osteoclastic bone resorption
Diagnostic workup: measure serum PTH, PTHrP, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
**Bisphosphonate-refractory hypercalcemia or severe renal failure:** administer denosumab (monoclonal antibody targeting RANKL)

UWSA1:Q139.boardCall: Post-bariatric surgery + rapid massive weight loss -> cholesterol supersaturation of bile -> symptomatic cholelithiasis (biliary colic/cholecystitis).
UWSA1:Q139.hinge: Rapid weight loss after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass increases biliary cholesterol secretion and impairs gallbladder motility, predisposing to gallstones.
UWSA1:Q139.trap: Anastomotic leak occurs within days to weeks post-surgery with fever, peritonitis, and septic shock, not recurrent postprandial RUQ colic 5 months later.

A.clue: Early postoperative disruption with peritonitis and sepsis
A.fit: Not here: recurrent postprandial right upper quadrant colic at 5 months

B.clue: Arterial or venous occlusion causing bowel wall ischemia
B.fit: Not here: pain is localized postprandial right upper quadrant tenderness
B.tempting: severe acute abdominal pain after surgery

C.clue: Hyperosmolar food bolus entering jejunum rapidly
C.fit: Not here: severe right upper quadrant colic radiating to shoulder

D.clue: Biliary cholesterol supersaturation from weight loss
D.fit: Here: 15-kg rapid weight loss after Roux-en-Y, postprandial RUQ pain radiating to shoulder, RUQ tenderness

E.clue: Retrograde reflux into gastric pouch
E.fit: Not here: causes substernal burning and regurgitation rather than severe episodic right upper quadrant biliary colic

algorithm.title: Cholelithiasis after rapid weight loss (Bariatric surgery)

nodes.text: Evaluate postprandial right upper quadrant pain radiating to shoulder following bariatric surgery
Recognize rapid massive weight loss as the primary risk factor promoting biliary cholesterol supersaturation and gallstone formation
Prophylaxis: treat with oral ursodeoxycholic acid (ursodiol) for 6 months postoperatively following bariatric surgery
Diagnostic imaging: perform right upper quadrant ultrasound to evaluate for gallstones, acoustic shadowing, and gallbladder wall thickening
**Symptomatic cholelithiasis or acute cholecystitis:** perform laparoscopic cholecystectomy
**Suspected choledocholithiasis:** note that altered anatomy precludes standard ERCP; use transgastric or surgical exploration

UWSA1:Q140.boardCall: Young boy + autism features (hand flapping, poor eye contact) + speech delay + dysmorphic facies (long face, prominent forehead, large ears) -> Fragile X syndrome (CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in FMR1).
UWSA1:Q140.hinge: CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene leads to hypermethylation and gene inactivation, causing Fragile X syndrome.
UWSA1:Q140.trap: MECP2 mutation causes Rett syndrome, which occurs almost exclusively in girls with developmental regression; Angelman/Prader-Willi involve 15q11-q13 imprinting.

A.clue: Trisomy 21 causing intellectual disability and hypotonia
A.fit: Not here: prominent forehead and large ears, not upslanting palpebral fissures

B.clue: Maternal 15q11-q13 deletion causing puppet-like ataxia
B.fit: Not here: inappropriate laughter, microcephaly, and ataxia rather than autistic behaviors, hand flapping, and large ears
B.tempting: severe speech impairment and hand flapping

C.clue: Paternal 15q11-q13 deletion causing hyperphagia and obesity
C.fit: Not here: prominent forehead and large ears, not neonatal hypotonia and obesity

D.clue: MECP2 loss-of-function mutation in young girls
D.fit: Not here: patient is male with prominent forehead and large ears

E.clue: CGG repeat expansion with hypermethylation of FMR1
E.fit: Here: 6-year-old boy with speech delay, poor eye contact, hand flapping, prominent forehead, large ears

nodes.text: Identify developmental delay, autism spectrum behaviors (hand flapping, poor eye contact), and dysmorphic features (large ears, long face)
Perform molecular genetic testing: identify CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion (> 200 repeats) in the FMR1 gene
Hypermethylation of the expanded FMR1 promoter halts transcription of fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP)
Comprehensive multidisciplinary intervention: speech therapy, occupational therapy, and specialized educational support
**Targeted pharmacological management:** treat severe ADHD symptoms with methylphenidate or anxiety/aggression with SSRIs
Post-pubertal monitoring: screen for macroorchidism, mitral valve prolapse, and provide genetic counseling to family members

UWSA1:Q141.boardCall: Glomerular hematuria (dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, brown urine) -> Quantification of urinary protein (24-hour urine protein or urine protein-to-creatinine ratio).
UWSA1:Q141.hinge: Identification of glomerular bleeding (RBC casts, dysmorphic RBCs) requires quantifying proteinuria to evaluate for glomerulonephritis or nephrotic-range disease.
UWSA1:Q141.trap: Nonglomerular hematuria (stones, cancer) requires CT urography and cystoscopy; glomerular hematuria does not require urological CT.

A.clue: Imaging for renal parenchymal masses or nephrolithiasis
A.fit: Not here: dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts localize bleeding to glomerulus; CT is for nonglomerular hematuria

B.clue: Quantifying proteinuria to assess glomerular damage severity
B.fit: Here: 34yo with reddish-brown urine, positive dipstick protein/blood, dysmorphic RBCs, and RBC casts

C.clue: No further diagnostic workup for benign hematuria
C.fit: Not here: presence of true red blood cell casts confirms active underlying glomerulonephritis requiring workup

D.clue: Microbiologic culture for bacterial cystitis or pyelonephritis
D.fit: Not here: dysmorphic erythrocytes and red cell casts indicate glomerulonephritis rather than bacterial tract infection

E.clue: Exfoliative urinary cytology for urothelial carcinoma
E.fit: Not here: dysmorphic red cells and casts localize bleeding to glomeruli, not bladder urothelium

nodes.text: Initial microscopic urinalysis: differentiate glomerular (dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts) from nonglomerular hematuria
Quantify urinary protein excretion with spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio or 24-hour urine collection
Check serum renal function (BUN/creatinine) and obtain baseline serum complement levels (C3, C4)
**Serologic autoimmune workup:** test ANA, anti-dsDNA, ANCA, anti-GBM, and serum/urine protein electrophoresis
**Significant proteinuria (> 1 g/day), elevated creatinine, or active nephritic sediment:** perform renal biopsy
Nonglomerular gross hematuria (clots, bright red): evaluate with CT urography and cystoscopy

UWSA1:Q142.boardCall: Elderly man living alone + dementia + ecchymoses + inflamed gums + pedal edema + normal platelets -> Malnutrition (Scurvy and mixed vitamin deficiencies).
UWSA1:Q142.hinge: Dementia-related self-neglect causing dietary deficiency of vitamin C (perifollicular ecchymoses, inflamed bleeding gums) and protein (hypoalbuminemic edema).
UWSA1:Q142.trap: Ecchymoses in an elderly person wandering outdoors suggests elder abuse or trauma, but inflamed gingiva and bilateral symmetric findings point to nutritional scurvy.

A.clue: Clonal stem cell neoplasm causing refractory cytopenias
A.fit: Not here: platelets are completely normal 150,000/mm3 and gums are inflamed from vitamin deficiency

B.clue: Primary adrenocortical failure with hyperkalemia and hypotension
B.fit: Not here: blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg and ecchymoses with inflamed gums point to scurvy

C.clue: Hepatic cirrhosis with impaired clotting factor synthesis
C.fit: Not here: lack of jaundice, spider angiomas, or ascites, with normal abdominal examination

D.clue: Systemic necrotizing small-vessel inflammatory vasculitis
D.fit: Not here: absence of palpable purpura, hematuria, or pulmonary findings; findings reflect vitamin C deficiency

E.clue: Multiple nutritional deficiencies from chronic dietary neglect
E.fit: Here: demented man living alone, bilateral ecchymoses, inflamed gums, pedal edema, normal platelets

F.clue: Non-accidental physical trauma in vulnerable elder
F.fit: Not here: symmetric bilateral ecchymoses, inflamed spongy gums, and edema reflect nutritional scurvy, not blunt trauma
F.tempting: unexplained bruising in a wandering elder

nodes.text: Identify clinical malnutrition in elderly: cognitive impairment, unintentional weight loss, edema, and mucosal/skin lesions
Recognize multiple vitamin deficiencies: scurvy (vitamin C deficiency: swollen gums, ecchymoses), folate/B12 deficiency, and protein-calorie wasting
Laboratory evaluation: check serum albumin, prealbumin, vitamin B12, folate, ascorbic acid, and INR
**Confirmed vitamin C deficiency:** prescribe oral vitamin C (ascorbic acid)
Initiate high-calorie, high-protein dietary plan and enroll in community meal delivery programs (Meals on Wheels)
Evaluate functional dependency: assess capacity to live independently and coordinate social work consultation

UWSA1:Q143.boardCall: End-stage renal disease + hypocalcemia + hyperphosphatemia + bone pain (renal osteodystrophy) -> Secondary hyperparathyroidism -> Parathyroid glandular hyperplasia.
UWSA1:Q143.hinge: Chronic phosphate retention and impaired 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D synthesis lead to hypocalcemia, causing compensatory hyperplasia of all four parathyroid glands.
UWSA1:Q143.trap: Single parathyroid adenoma causes primary hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcemia; ESRD causes secondary hyperplasia of all glands with low/normal calcium.

A.clue: Autoimmune destruction of parathyroid glands causing hypocalcemia
A.fit: Not here: ESRD induces compensatory parathyroid hormone hypersecretion, not autoimmune gland destruction

B.clue: Noncaseating granulomatous invasion of parathyroid tissue
B.fit: Not here: sarcoidosis causes hypercalcemia via extrarenal calcitriol synthesis, not hypocalcemia with bone pain

C.clue: Glandular involution secondary to autonomous hypercalcemia
C.fit: Not here: hypocalcemia (7.9 mg/dL) stimulates parathyroid proliferation, leading to glandular hyperplasia

D.clue: Four-gland cellular hyperplasia driven by hypocalcemia
D.fit: Here: ESRD on hemodialysis, bone pain, low calcium 7.9 mg/dL, high phosphorus 6.1 mg/dL

E.clue: Autonomous solitary adenoma causing primary hyperparathyroidism
E.fit: Not here: single adenoma causes hypercalcemia; ESRD induces diffuse four-gland hyperplasia with low calcium

algorithm.title: Secondary hyperparathyroidism in chronic kidney disease

nodes.text: Identify chronic kidney disease-mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD): hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and renal osteodystrophy
Reduced 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and phosphate retention stimulate diffuse four-gland parathyroid glandular hyperplasia
Initial medical therapy: dietary phosphate restriction and oral phosphate binders (sevelamer, calcium carbonate) with meals
Administer active vitamin D sterols (calcitriol or paricalcitol) or calcimimetics (cinacalcet) to suppress PTH secretion
**Target intact PTH:** maintain levels between 2 and 9 times the upper limit of normal for stage 5 CKD
**Tertiary hyperparathyroidism (refractory hypercalcemia):** perform subtotal parathyroidectomy

UWSA1:Q144.boardCall: Severe acute delirium with combativeness threatening safety -> low-dose oral or intramuscular haloperidol.
UWSA1:Q144.hinge: When an acutely delirious patient is combative and poses an immediate threat to self or staff, low-dose antipsychotic (haloperidol) is indicated.
UWSA1:Q144.trap: Benzodiazepines (lorazepam) paradoxically worsen delirium and increase fall risk, and are indicated only for alcohol or sedative withdrawal.

A.clue: First-generation high-potency antipsychotic for acute agitation
A.fit: Here: combative delirious elderly patient striking staff and pulling IV lines due to UTI

B.clue: GABA-A agonist sedating patients with withdrawal delirium
B.fit: Not here: benzodiazepines paradoxically worsen delirium and increase fall risk in non-withdrawal delirium

C.clue: Indwelling urethral catheter drainage
C.fit: Not here: indwelling catheters are invasive tethers that exacerbate delirium and promote secondary infections

D.clue: Confronting and directly debating delusional beliefs
D.fit: Not here: directly challenging delusions provokes greater combativeness and emotional distress in delirium

E.clue: Cholinesterase inhibitor for chronic Alzheimer dementia
E.fit: Not here: donepezil treats chronic dementia, not acute medical delirium

F.clue: Physical wrist or limb restraints
F.fit: Not here: physical restraints worsen agitation, increase struggle, and carry high risk of strangulation and asphyxiation

nodes.text: Identify acute delirium: fluctuating cognitive impairment, inattention, and perceptual disturbances triggered by medical illness
First-line nonpharmacological de-escalation: frequent reorientation, family presence, sitter, quiet room, and minimize tethers
Administer low-dose haloperidol for severe acute agitation threatening self or staff safety (physical violence, pulling lines)
**Alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal delirium:** administer intravenous lorazepam or diazepam instead of antipsychotics
**Urinary tract infection present:** initiate empiric antibacterial therapy
Review and discontinue deliriogenic medications: anticholinergics, sedatives, opioids, and antihistamines

UWSA1:Q145.boardCall: Cirrhosis + ascites + ascitic absolute neutrophil count ≥ 250/mm3 -> Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis -> IV third-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime or ceftriaxone) + IV albumin.
UWSA1:Q145.hinge: Ascitic fluid polymorphonuclear count ≥ 250/mm3 is diagnostic of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, requiring immediate empiric intravenous antibiotics.
UWSA1:Q145.trap: Furosemide or large-volume paracentesis worsens intravascular volume depletion and prerenal azotemia during active peritonitis.

A.clue: Loop diuretic for cirrhotic fluid overload
A.fit: Not here: diuretics cause intravascular volume contraction and precipitate hepatorenal syndrome during active infection

B.clue: Empiric intravenous third-generation cephalosporin for SBP
B.fit: Here: cirrhotic patient with lethargy and ascitic PMN count 360/mm3 (400 × 90%)

C.clue: Nonselective beta blocker for variceal bleeding prophylaxis
C.fit: Not here: beta blockers reduce cardiac output and are held during acute sepsis/SBP to avoid shock

D.clue: Therapeutic drainage of large volume ascitic fluid
D.fit: Not here: therapeutic paracentesis is not indicated for acute peritonitis; immediate antibiotic therapy is required

E.clue: Interventional portosystemic shunt for refractory portal hypertension
E.fit: Not here: active spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is an absolute contraindication to elective TIPS placement

nodes.text: Perform diagnostic paracentesis in all cirrhotic patients with ascites and fever, abdominal pain, or unexplained encephalopathy
Confirm SBP: ascitic fluid absolute neutrophil count (ANC) ≥ 250/mm3 (total WBC × % neutrophils)
Initiate immediate empiric intravenous antibiotic therapy: third-generation cephalosporin (IV ceftriaxone or cefotaxime)
Administer intravenous albumin on days 1 and 3 to prevent hepatorenal syndrome and reduce mortality
**Active acute infection:** discontinue nonselective beta blockers to prevent hemodynamic deterioration
Initiate lifelong secondary antimicrobial prophylaxis upon discharge: oral daily trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or ciprofloxacin

UWSA1:Q146.boardCall: Elderly man + bicytopenia/pancytopenia + macrocytosis + dysplastic hyposegmented neutrophils -> Myelodysplastic syndrome -> Bone marrow biopsy.
UWSA1:Q146.hinge: Macrocytic anemia with dysplastic neutrophil hyposegmentation (Pelger-Huët anomaly) and thrombocytopenia warrants bone marrow biopsy to confirm myelodysplastic syndrome.
UWSA1:Q146.trap: Normal vitamin B12 rules out cobalamin deficiency; ovalomacrocytosis with neutrophil hyposegmentation (not hypersegmentation) points away from nutritional megaloblastosis toward MDS.

A.clue: Autoantibody confirming pernicious anemia
A.fit: Not here: serum vitamin B12 level is normal, and dysplastic neutrophils show reduced (not hyper-) segmentation
A.tempting: macrocytic anemia in an older adult

B.clue: Toxic heavy metal assay for plumbism
B.fit: Not here: lead toxicity typically causes microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling, not macrocytosis and Pelger-Huët cells

C.clue: Marrow aspiration and biopsy evaluating hematopoietic dysplasia
C.fit: Here: 66yo with fatigue, macrocytic anemia (Hb 7.5, MCV 106), thrombocytopenia, and hyposegmented neutrophils

D.clue: Renal hormone assay for anemia of kidney disease
D.fit: Not here: normal renal function, dysplastic cells indicate clonal marrow neoplasm

E.clue: Metabolite assay detecting subtle tissue B12 deficiency
E.fit: Not here: normal B12 with thrombocytopenia and neutrophil hyposegmentation confirms MDS rather than B12 deficiency

F.clue: Electrophoresis screening for paraproteinemic disorders
F.fit: Not here: dysplastic hyposegmented neutrophils and thrombocytopenia point to myelodysplasia rather than plasma cell myeloma

nodes.text: Suspect myelodysplastic syndrome in an older patient with unexplained cytopenias and macrocytic anemia
Review peripheral blood smear demonstrating dysplastic changes (ovalomacrocytes, hyposegmented/hypogranulated neutrophils)
Perform bone marrow aspiration and biopsy with cytogenetics to confirm hypercellular marrow, dysplasia, and blast count
**Risk stratification:** use revised International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS-R) based on cytogenetics, blasts, and cytopenias
**Lower-risk MDS:** supportive transfusions + erythropoiesis-stimulating agents or luspatercept for transfusion dependence
**Higher-risk MDS or excess blasts:** treat with hypomethylating agents (azacitidine, decitabine) or allogeneic stem cell transplantation

UWSA1:Q147.boardCall: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy + elevated postvoid residual (> 300 mL) + overflow incontinence -> Intermittent self-catheterization.
UWSA1:Q147.hinge: High postvoid residual volume (> 200-300 mL) confirms neurogenic overflow incontinence; clean intermittent self-catheterization is the definitive treatment to drain the bladder.
UWSA1:Q147.trap: Muscarinic antagonists (oxybutynin) treat urge incontinence and are strictly contraindicated in overflow incontinence because they exacerbate urinary retention.

A.clue: Beta-3 adrenergic agonist relaxing detrusor smooth muscle
A.fit: Not here: mirabegron relaxes detrusor muscle, which would worsen urinary retention and overflow dribbling

B.clue: Periodic clean urethral catheterization to empty bladder
B.fit: Here: long-standing diabetic with suprapubic fullness, nocturnal dribbling, and postvoid residual volume 300 mL

C.clue: Suburethral synthetic mesh sling supporting bladder neck
C.fit: Not here: surgical sling is indicated for stress incontinence with urethral hypermobility, not neurogenic overflow

D.clue: Anticholinergic agent suppressing detrusor involuntary contractions
D.fit: Not here: antimuscarinics (oxybutynin) paralyze detrusor contractility and precipitate acute urinary retention in overflow

E.clue: Kegel exercises strengthening pelvic floor musculature
E.fit: Not here: pelvic floor training improves stress and urge incontinence but cannot treat neurogenic detrusor underactivity

F.clue: Antidepressant with anticholinergic and adrenergic bladder actions
F.fit: Not here: imipramine has potent anticholinergic effects that further impair detrusor emptying in overflow incontinence

nodes.text: Measure postvoid residual (PVR) volume via ultrasound or straight catheterization in patients with urinary dribbling
Confirm overflow incontinence: elevated postvoid residual volume > 150-200 mL in women (> 50-100 mL in men)
Initiate clean intermittent self-catheterization (CIC) to decompress the bladder and protect upper urinary tract function
**Behavioral voiding strategies:** add scheduled timed voiding every 2-3 hours and Crede maneuver (suprapubic pressure)
**Contraindicated medications:** avoid anticholinergic/muscarinic antagonists and tricyclics, which paralyze detrusor contractility
Screen for secondary complications: monitor for recurrent urinary tract infections, hydronephrosis, and progressive renal insufficiency

UWSA1:Q148.boardCall: Elderly patient (> 70) + systolic ejection murmur at right upper sternal border -> Aortic stenosis secondary to age-related calcification of valvular leaflets.
UWSA1:Q148.hinge: Age-related dystrophic calcification and fibrocalcific remodeling of trileaflet aortic valves is the leading etiology of aortic stenosis in patients > 70 years.
UWSA1:Q148.trap: Vegetations cause acute infective endocarditis with regurgitant murmurs and systemic fever; dystrophic calcification is the mechanism of chronic senile stenosis.

A.fit: Here: 72yo man with asymptomatic crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at right upper sternal border

B.clue: Infective endocarditis with thrombotic valvular vegetation
B.fit: Not here: asymptomatic active 72-year-old walking 3 miles/day without fever, chills, or systemic illness

**Confidence interval includes 0 (null value):** pairwise difference is not statistically significant

algorithm.title: Calculating odds ratios in case-control studies

nodes.text: Construct 2x2 contingency table: disease status (columns) vs exposure status (rows)
Assign cell counts: a = exposed cases, b = exposed controls, c = unexposed cases, d = unexposed controls
Compute odds ratio using cross-product: OR = (a * d) / (b * c)
**OR = 1.0:** exposure is not associated with altered odds of disease
**OR > 1.0:** exposure is associated with increased odds of disease
**OR < 1.0:** exposure is associated with decreased odds of disease
Interpret 95% confidence interval: statistically significant if interval excludes 1.0

nodes.text: Recognize interstitial lung disease: progressive exertional dyspnea, dry cough, bibasilar fine crackles

Replace potassium and initiate mineralocorticoid antagonist (spironolactone)

UWSA1:Q086.hinge: Severe insulin deficiency promotes peripheral lipolysis, delivering free fatty acids to the liver for conversion into ketones.
UWSA1:Q086.trap: Lipolysis is driven by elevated catecholamines and glucagon, not decreased catecholamine levels.

A.clue: Hepatic beta-oxidation generating acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate
A.fit: Here: diabetic ketoacidosis with high anion gap metabolic acidosis and ketosis

B.clue: Skeletal muscle glycogen breakdown releasing glucose
B.fit: Not here: skeletal muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase and does not generate ketoacidosis

C.clue: Proximal renal tubular acidosis (type 2 RTA)
C.fit: Not here: high anion gap acidosis with prominent ketonemia rather than normal gap RTA

D.clue: Distal renal tubular acidosis (type 1 RTA)
D.fit: Not here: marked elevated anion gap > 14 and profound ketosis from insulin deficiency

E.clue: Renal clearance buffering metabolic ketoacidosis
E.fit: Not here: renal excretion eliminates excess acid and does not generate metabolic acidosis

F.clue: Fat breakdown mediated by reduced catecholamine tone
F.fit: Not here: lipolysis in DKA is driven by markedly elevated, not decreased, catecholamines

nodes.text: Absolute insulin deficiency leads to uninhibited lipolysis and release of free fatty acids
Hepatic uptake of fatty acids leads to beta-oxidation and breakdown into ketoacids (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate)
Accumulation of circulating ketoacids causes elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis and Kussmaul respirations
Resuscitate with intravenous isotonic crystalloid fluids (0.9% normal saline) to restore intravascular volume
Initiate continuous intravenous regular insulin infusion to suppress ketogenesis and normalize blood glucose
Add potassium to intravenous fluids once serum potassium is < 5.3 mEq/L to prevent fatal hypokalemia

responsible for this patient's symptoms
patient's symptoms

UWSA1:Q087.boardCall: DKA following initial fluid bolus + K 4.4 mEq/L -> IV regular insulin infusion + IV fluids with potassium.
UWSA1:Q087.hinge: Once initial fluid resuscitation is complete and potassium is between 3.3 and 5.3 mEq/L, start IV regular insulin plus potassium.
UWSA1:Q087.trap: Glucose is 360 mg/dL, so dextrose is withheld until glucose falls to ≤ 200 mg/dL to prevent cerebral edema.

A.clue: Isotonic saline maintenance without insulin or potassium
A.fit: Not here: insulin is mandatory to halt ketogenesis and potassium is needed to prevent hypokalemia

B.clue: Sodium bicarbonate for severe acidemia
B.fit: Not here: venous pH is 7.2

C.clue: Insulin infusion with dextrose-containing fluids
C.fit: Not here: serum glucose is 360 mg/dL (dextrose added only when glucose ≤ 200 mg/dL)

D.clue: Continuous IV regular insulin with potassium repletion
D.fit: Here: post-bolus glucose 360, potassium 4.4 mEq/L, persistent ketonuria, pH 7.2

E.clue: Basal subcutaneous insulin during acute DKA
E.fit: Not here: acute DKA requires continuous IV regular insulin infusion rather than subcutaneous depot

F.clue: Subcutaneous short-acting insulin with oral potassium
F.fit: Not here: variable absorption in dehydrated patient necessitates continuous intravenous infusion

nodes.text: Initiate volume resuscitation with isotonic saline bolus over 1 hour
Start continuous intravenous regular insulin infusion with potassium-supplemented intravenous fluids
**Serum potassium < 3.3 mEq/L:** hold insulin and administer IV potassium until K > 3.3 mEq/L
**Serum glucose ≤ 200 mg/dL:** add 5% dextrose to intravenous fluids to prevent hypoglycemia and cerebral edema
**Severe acidemia with pH < 6.9:** consider slow infusion of isotonic sodium bicarbonate
Transition to subcutaneous insulin when anion gap closes (< 12 mEq/L), bicarbonate ≥ 15 mEq/L, and patient tolerates oral intake

triggers.text: receives 10 mL/kg of normal saline over 1 hour
Point-of-care urinalysis continues to show large ketones
Potassium 4.4 mEq/L
Glucose 360 mg/dL

UWSA1:Q088.boardCall: Chemotherapy nadir + fever ≥ 38.3 C + severe neutropenia (leukocytes 600/mm3) -> Systemic bacterial infection (neutropenic fever).
UWSA1:Q088.hinge: Febrile neutropenia 10 days post-chemotherapy is caused by systemic bacterial translocation across disrupted mucosal barriers.
UWSA1:Q088.trap: Chemotherapy, stents, or transfusion could suggest drug reaction or delayed hemolysis, but acute fever and profound neutropenia define neutropenic fever.

A.clue: Hypersensitivity drug reaction with fever and rash
A.fit: Not here: lack of rash, wheezing, or eosinophilia, with severe life-threatening neutropenia

B.clue: Anamnestic antibody-mediated extravascular hemolysis
B.fit: Not here: lack of jaundice, elevated indirect bilirubin, or direct antiglobulin positivity

C.clue: Cytokine release from bulky neoplastic tissue
C.fit: Not here: acute high fever and septic shock presentation during post-chemotherapy nadir

D.clue: Hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, and hyperphosphatemia from cell lysis
D.fit: Not here: fever and neutropenia 10 days post-chemotherapy rather than immediate metabolic collapse

E.clue: Bacterial invasion during post-chemotherapy neutrophil nadir
E.fit: Here: fever 38.9 C, pulse 120, chemotherapy 10 days ago, leukocytes 600/mm3

nodes.text: Recognize febrile neutropenia: single oral temperature ≥ 38.3 C (101 F) with absolute neutrophil count < 500/mm3
Obtain immediate blood cultures from peripheral sites and indwelling central catheters
Promptly administer empiric broad-spectrum antipseudomonal monotherapy: cefepime, meropenem, or piperacillin-tazobactam
**Hemodynamic instability, catheter infection, or MRSA colonization:** add intravenous vancomycin
**Persistent fever after 4-7 days of antibacterial therapy:** add empiric antifungal therapy (voriconazole, caspofungin, or amphotericin B)
Continue antimicrobial therapy until neutrophil recovery (ANC > 500/mm3) and resolution of infection

Temperature is 38.9 C (102 F)
Leukocytes 600/mm3
decreased oral intake and confusion
pulse is 120/min

UWSA1:Q089.boardCall: Woman > 40 + BMI 31 + epigastric/RUQ pain + fever + leukocytosis + normal lipase -> Acute cholecystitis.
UWSA1:Q089.hinge: Fever, leukocytosis, and acute constant epigastric pain with normal lipase and mildly elevated ALT indicate cystic duct obstruction.
UWSA1:Q089.trap: Epigastric pain radiating to back suggests pancreatitis, but serum lipase is completely normal.

A.clue: Cystic duct stone impaction with inflammation
A.fit: Here: 42yo woman, epigastric pain, fever 38.2 C, WBC 14,000, normal lipase

B.clue: Hepatocellular necroinflammation with transaminases in thousands
B.fit: Not here: transaminases AST 37 and ALT 79 are only minimally elevated
B.tempting: fever and mildly elevated liver enzymes

C.clue: Pancreatic acinar autodigestion with elevated lipase
C.fit: Not here: completely normal serum lipase level rules out acute pancreatitis
C.tempting: severe epigastric pain radiating to back

D.clue: Extrahepatic biliary obstruction with high direct bilirubin
D.fit: Not here: normal total bilirubin 1.0 mg/dL and alkaline phosphatase 90 U/L

E.clue: Chronic gastritis or peptic ulcer disease
E.fit: Not here: acute fever 38.2 C and leukocytosis 14,000/mm3 with systemic toxicity

F.clue: Statin-induced hepatic or muscular toxicity
F.fit: Not here: acute fever and leukocytosis with localized peritoneal signs

G.clue: Malignant pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
G.fit: Not here: acute 3-hour onset with fever and leukocytosis in a 42-year-old
G.tempting: epigastric pain radiating to the back

nodes.text: Initial imaging: perform right upper quadrant abdominal ultrasound to assess gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, and stones
**Equivocal ultrasound findings:** perform cholescintigraphy (HIDA scan) showing gallbladder nonvisualization
Maintain bowel rest (NPO) + intravenous fluids + IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (ceftriaxone + metronidazole)
Perform early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 72 hours of symptom onset
**Critically ill or high surgical risk patients:** place percutaneous cholecystostomy tube for gallbladder drainage
Monitor for complications: gallbladder gangrene, perforation, emphysematous cholecystitis, or gallstone ileus

UWSA1:Q090.boardCall: Tension pneumothorax decompression -> decreases intrathoracic pressure -> increases systemic venous return (preload).
UWSA1:Q090.hinge: Decompressing trapped intrathoracic air relieves vena caval compression, restoring cardiac venous return and cardiac output.
UWSA1:Q090.trap: Restoring blood pressure may suggest increased contractility or vascular resistance, but the primary hemodynamic benefit is restoring venous return.

A.clue: Alveolar pressure remaining at end expiration
A.fit: Not here: needle decompression vents pleural air and does not increase PEEP

B.clue: Total circulating blood and fluid volume
B.fit: Not here: thoracostomy decompresses trapped air and does not administer fluid volume

C.clue: Inherent myocardial inotropic force
C.fit: Not here: intervention relieves external mechanical vascular compression without altering inotropy

D.clue: Resistance to forward blood flow from arterioles
D.fit: Not here: relieving obstructive shock increases cardiac output rather than systemic resistance

E.clue: Blood flow returning to the right atrium
E.fit: Here: tension pneumothorax with hypotension, tracheal deviation, absent sounds relieved by decompression

nodes.text: Recognize tension pneumothorax: respiratory distress, hypotension, unilateral absent breath sounds, and contralateral tracheal deviation
High intrathoracic pressure collapses the inferior and superior vena cava, severely impeding venous return and cardiac output
Perform emergent needle thoracostomy decompression in 2nd intercostal space (midclavicular) or 5th intercostal space (anterior axillary)
Immediate chest tube insertion (tube thoracostomy) following needle decompression for definitive evacuation of pleural air
Administer high-flow supplemental oxygen via nonrebreather mask + intravenous fluid resuscitation
Obtain follow-up chest radiograph to confirm complete lung re-expansion and proper chest tube positioning

Pulse oximetry is 88% on room air
neck veins are distended and the trachea is deviated to the right
Breath sounds are absent on the left side

abdominal-aortic-aneurysm.name: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
abdominal-aortic-aneurysm.scope: screening recommendations (men 65-75 who smoked), ultrasound imaging, surveillance intervals, elective repair thresholds, rupture
abdominal-aortic-aneurysm.core: Older adult with abdominal aortic dilation may remain asymptomatic until expansion or rupture; sudden abdominal/back pain and hypotension require immediate vascular rescue.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking strongest modifiable risk; older age, male sex, family history, hypertension, atherosclerosis
Women have higher rupture risk at smaller diameters; most aneurysms infrarenal

rows.label: Clues
items: Incidental pulsatile expansile abdominal mass; localized persistent pain suggests symptomatic aneurysm
Rupture triad incompletely present; transient stability may reflect contained retroperitoneal hemorrhage
Blue toe/distal ischemia may result from mural thrombus embolization

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Medial elastin/collagen degradation → progressive enlargement; greater wall radius increases tension
Retroperitoneal containment can briefly limit blood loss before catastrophic decompensation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Abdominal ultrasound** diagnoses AAA, generally diameter ≥3 cm; no contrast required
★ Stable suspected rupture or preoperative planning → **CT angiography**
Unstable suspected rupture → bedside ultrasound if immediate; no CT transport delaying surgery
Ultrasound detects aneurysm but cannot reliably exclude rupture; follow symptoms/hemodynamics

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Rupture → **urgent vascular repair**, IV access, blood products; avoid delaying for complete workup
Permissive hypotension during transfer/resuscitation until hemorrhage control when clinically feasible
★ Elective repair at **≥5.5 cm men, ≥5.0 cm women**, or aneurysm-attributable symptoms
Rapid growth ≥0.5 cm/6 months → repair consideration; endovascular versus open based on anatomy/fitness
Smaller asymptomatic lesions → ultrasound surveillance below; refer vascular surgery, manage cardiovascular risks

rows.label: Complications
items: Rupture, thrombosis, distal embolization; repair → AKI, bowel ischemia, endoleak after EVAR
Aortoenteric fistula after prior graft: herald GI bleed → catastrophic hemorrhage; urgent evaluation

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ USPSTF: **one-time ultrasound men 65–75 who ever smoked**; selectively screen never-smoking men
Women never smoked/no family history → no screening; women smokers/family history → USPSTF evidence insufficient
Smoking cessation, BP control, statin for atherosclerotic disease; lifelong imaging follow-up after EVAR

rows.label: Mimics
items: Renal colic: flank-to-groin pain, hematuria; shock atypical
Aortic dissection: abrupt chest/back pain, possible pulse deficits or branch ischemia

acid-base-disorders.name: Acid-base disorders
acid-base-disorders.scope: Metabolic acidosis (anion gap, non-anion gap), metabolic alkalosis (saline-responsive vs saline-resistant), respiratory acidosis, respiratory alkalosis, Winter formula, mixed disorders
acid-base-disorders.core: Identify the primary pH disturbance, test expected compensation, then investigate the anion gap or urine chloride to locate the cause.

rows.label: Definition
items: Acidemia: pH <7.35; alkalemia: >7.45; normal pH can hide opposing primary disorders
Metabolic: primary HCO3 change; respiratory: primary PaCO2 change

rows.label: Formula
items: ★ **AG = Na − (Cl + HCO3)**; usual normal ≈8–12, laboratory dependent
Hypoalbuminemia correction: add 2.5 to AG per 1 g/dL albumin below 4
★ **Winter: expected PaCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3 + 8 ±2**

rows.label: Interpret
items: HCO3 12 → expected PaCO2 26 ±2; measured 40 → additional respiratory acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis: expected PaCO2 ≈40 + 0.7 × (HCO3 − 24), ±5
Respiratory HCO3 change per 10 PaCO2: acidosis +1 acute/+4 chronic; alkalosis −2 acute/−4 chronic

rows.label: Use when
items: ★ Alkalosis: **urine Cl <20 mmol/L** → saline-responsive; ≥20 → diuretics/mineralocorticoids
ΔAG exceeds HCO3 fall → additional alkalosis; smaller ΔAG → additional non-gap acidosis

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Compensation never overshoots; values outside expected range imply **mixed disorder**
Salicylates often cause respiratory alkalosis plus high-gap acidosis; near-normal pH is deceptive
Diarrhea/RTA: non-gap acidosis; renal failure: either gap pattern

acid-base-disorders.evidence: Established physiologic formulas; no guideline involved.

acute-coronary-syndromes.name: Acute coronary syndromes
acute-coronary-syndromes.scope: Unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI, cardiac biomarkers, risk stratification (HEART/TIMI), antiplatelet and anticoagulation, reperfusion
acute-coronary-syndromes.core: Acute myocardial ischemia from coronary plaque disruption: distinguish occlusive infarction needing immediate reperfusion from non-ST-elevation syndromes needing risk-guided invasive management.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, CKD, age, premature family CAD
Cocaine/stimulants, anemia, tachyarrhythmia may provoke ischemia; distinguish supply-demand injury from plaque rupture

rows.label: Clues
items: Pressure with arm/jaw radiation, diaphoresis, nausea; older adults/diabetes may have dyspnea alone
Inferior MI with hypotension, clear lungs, raised JVP → suspect RV infarction
★ New murmur, pulmonary edema, shock after MI → **mechanical complication**, urgent echo

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Platelet activation and thrombin-mediated clot reduce coronary perfusion; necrosis releases troponin
Type 2 MI: oxygen mismatch without acute atherothrombosis; treat precipitating cause

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ECG within 10 minutes**, repeat if nondiagnostic; serial high-sensitivity troponin using validated pathway
Posterior suspicion → V7–V9; inferior MI → right-sided leads; new LBBB alone insufficient for STEMI
★ **Do not wait for troponin before STEMI reperfusion**; bedside echo if diagnosis/complications uncertain
HEART ≤3 + negative serial troponins → low risk; TIMI/GRACE stratifies NSTE-ACS

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Chewed aspirin**, P2Y12 inhibitor, anticoagulant such as heparin, high-intensity atorvastatin; oxygen only if hypoxemic
Nitroglycerin for pain unless hypotension, RV infarction, or recent PDE5 inhibitor; avoid NSAIDs
★ STEMI → **primary PCI** within 90 minutes at PCI center, ≤120 minutes including transfer
IF PCI delay >120 minutes, symptoms <12 hours, no contraindication → fibrinolysis promptly, then transfer

rows.label: Complications
items: VT/VF, AV block, HF, cardiogenic shock; papillary rupture, septal rupture, free-wall rupture
Later aneurysm/thrombus, embolism, Dressler syndrome; antithrombotics → bleeding

rows.label: Prevention
items: DAPT usually 12 months after ACS unless bleeding risk changes plan; cardiac rehabilitation, smoking cessation
ACE inhibitor/ARB for LV dysfunction; beta-blocker when stable, avoid in shock or acute decompensation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Aortic dissection: abrupt tearing pain/pulse deficit; anticoagulation or lysis dangerous
Pericarditis: positional pleuritic pain, diffuse changes
PE: hypoxemia, thrombotic risk, RV strain

table.title: Syndrome branches
rows: Urgent catheterization if unstable; otherwise risk-guided angiography
Regional ST elevation or occlusion equivalent
Prior intracranial hemorrhage, active bleeding, suspected dissection

adult-immunizations.name: Adult immunizations
adult-immunizations.scope: Routine adult vaccines, immunocompromised and HIV, pregnancy, live-vaccine contraindications, chronic medical conditions (COPD, diabetes, liver disease), vaccine counseling and addressing hesitancy
adult-immunizations.core: Match vaccination to age, prior doses, pregnancy, immune status, and exposure risk; missed series resume without restarting.

rows.label: Who
items: ★ **HepB**: all adults 19–59; ≥60 with risk or requesting protection
Liver disease → HepA/HepB; COPD, diabetes, smoking → pneumococcal before routine age
Asplenia → pneumococcal, MenACWY, MenB, Hib; HIV → MenACWY

rows.label: Start/stop
items: ★ Pregnancy: **Tdap each pregnancy at 27–36 wk**; inactivated influenza any trimester
Maternal RSV: Abrysvo at 32–36 wk, September–January; previous pregnancy dose → infant antibody instead
RSV once: all ≥75; ages 50–74 with increased severe-disease risk

rows.label: Test
items: Review records, contraindications, immunity; HBV serology useful, but **do not delay vaccination**
★ Immunocompromised ≥19 → recombinant zoster; HIV CD4 ≥200 permits MMR/varicella if nonimmune
HPV started <15 → two doses; ≥15 or immunocompromised → three

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Avoid live MMR, varicella, intranasal influenza** during pregnancy or severe immunosuppression
PCV15 → PPSV23: minimum 8 weeks if immunocompromised; mild illness/antibiotics need no deferral
Hesitancy → elicit concern, explain benefit, recommend clearly; refusal → document, revisit

table.title: Routine adult schedule
rows: Annual influenza; updated COVID-19 for all adults
Tdap once, then either every 10 years
PCV20/21 alone; PCV15 → PPSV23 after 1 year

alcohol-withdrawal.name: Alcohol withdrawal
alcohol-withdrawal.core: Autonomic and neuropsychiatric excitation after reducing prolonged heavy alcohol intake; progression from mild symptoms to life-threatening delirium.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior withdrawal seizures/delirium, repeated detoxifications, heavy sustained use, older age
Acute illness, electrolyte depletion, concurrent sedative dependence; poor support increases outpatient failure

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, insomnia, nausea; symptoms possible with **positive blood alcohol**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Chronic ethanol → downregulated GABA inhibition/upregulated NMDA excitation; cessation unmasks neuronal hyperactivity
Repeated episodes → kindling, progressively lower seizure threshold

rows.label: Dx
items: **Clinical diagnosis** + time since reduction; bedside glucose, CBC, electrolytes, Mg, phosphate, liver tests
★ **CIWA-Ar** if communicative; ≥19 severe; delirium/intubation → **RASS/MINDS**
First/focal seizure, head injury, focal deficit, atypical timing → head CT; do not assume withdrawal

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Diazepam/chlordiazepoxide** symptom-triggered; liver dysfunction/older frail adults → **lorazepam/oxazepam**
★ Seizures/delirium → monitored inpatient **IV benzodiazepines**; refractory → ICU phenobarbital with respiratory monitoring
★ **Parenteral thiamine**; hypoglycemia → immediate dextrose, never wait; correct electrolyte deficits
Phenytoin ineffective; antipsychotics/clonidine/dexmedetomidine adjuncts only, without seizure protection

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration, dysrhythmias, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis; excessive sedation → respiratory depression
Malnutrition → Wernicke encephalopathy: confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia; suspected → high-dose IV thiamine

rows.label: Prevention
items: High-risk inpatients → preventive benzodiazepines; outpatient withdrawal only if mild, reliable supervision
Recovery: **naltrexone** unless opioids/acute hepatitis; **acamprosate** unless severe CKD; addiction follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hepatic encephalopathy: asterixis, decompensated cirrhosis, less autonomic excitation
Sepsis: infectious source, hypotension, persistent inflammatory findings
Sedative withdrawal: benzodiazepine/barbiturate reduction; similar syndrome, different exposure

table.title: Approximate onset after reduction; overlap common

amenorrhea.name: Amenorrhea
amenorrhea.scope: Primary amenorrhea (Turner syndrome, Mullerian agenesis, AIS), secondary amenorrhea (pregnancy, functional hypothalamic, hyperprolactinemia, thyroid, premature ovarian insufficiency, Asherman), diagnostic algorithm
amenorrhea.core: Absent menses requires pregnancy exclusion, then assessment of anatomy, estrogen status, thyroid function, prolactin, and the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Weight loss, intense exercise, psychosocial stress; pituitary disease, dopamine-blocking drugs, thyroid dysfunction
Uterine instrumentation, chemotherapy, autoimmune disease; congenital reproductive tract or chromosomal abnormalities

rows.label: Clues
items: Primary: no menarche by 15; absent breast development by 13 also warrants evaluation
Secondary: ≥3 months absent previously regular cycles, or ≥6 months previously irregular
Galactorrhea/headache, visual symptoms, hot flashes, hirsutism, cyclic pelvic pain guide localization
