items: ATN: muddy-brown casts after ischemia/toxins
Urologic bleeding: isomorphic RBCs, clots, no RBC casts

glomerulonephritis.evidence: Not checked online; established nephrology teaching.

gout.name: Gout and crystal arthropathy
gout.scope: Acute gout, chronic gout and urate lowering, pseudogout (CPPD)
gout.core: Abrupt intensely painful inflammatory arthritis from crystal deposition; gout and CPPD require different long-term prevention despite similar flare management.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Gout: CKD, obesity, alcohol, purines/fructose, thiazide/loop diuretics, low-dose aspirin
CPPD: older age, joint injury, hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypomagnesemia
Flares follow surgery, dehydration, illness, or changes in urate concentration

rows.label: Clues
items: Rapid-onset red swollen tender joint, often overnight; fever possible
Chronic gout: tophi on ears/olecranon, erosive arthritis; recurrent flares separated by asymptomatic intervals
CPPD in younger adults → investigate associated metabolic disorders

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Crystal phagocytosis activates inflammasome/IL-1 → neutrophilic synovitis
Most hyperuricemia reflects reduced renal urate excretion rather than excessive production

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ First/atypical acute monoarthritis → **arthrocentesis**, polarized microscopy, Gram stain/culture
★ **Crystals do not exclude septic arthritis**; serum urate may be normal during gout flare
Chronic imaging: punched-out defects with overhanging edges; ultrasound double-contour sign supports urate deposition

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute either crystal flare → **NSAID, colchicine, or glucocorticoid**; intraarticular steroid only after infection excluded
CKD/ulcer/anticoagulation → favor steroid; adjust colchicine for renal impairment/interactions; avoid NSAIDs in advanced CKD
★ Urate lowering: **allopurinol first-line**, including CKD; start low, titrate to serum urate <6 mg/dL
Continue urate lowering during flares; may start during treated flare; no routine asymptomatic-hyperuricemia treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Gout: destructive arthritis, uric-acid stones; CPPD: chronic degenerative/inflammatory arthropathy
Allopurinol hypersensitivity; colchicine → diarrhea/neuromyopathy
Xanthine-oxidase inhibitors + azathioprine/6-MP → severe marrow suppression

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Urate lowering: **tophi, joint damage, ≥2 flares/year**; first flare with CKD ≥3/stones/urate >9 → consider
Starting urate lowering → colchicine/NSAID prophylaxis 3–6 months; serial urate monitoring
Weight reduction, limit alcohol/fructose; replace thiazide with losartan when feasible; retain indicated aspirin
Before allopurinol: HLA-B*58:01 testing with Southeast Asian/African American ancestry; CPPD lacks crystal-depleting drugs

rows.label: Mimics
items: Septic arthritis: positive culture, bacteremia risk; aspiration essential when uncertain
Cellulitis: superficial inflammation, less restriction of passive joint motion
RA: persistent symmetric small-joint synovitis

gout.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACR gout guideline 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10563586/), [ACR gout education 2025](https://rheumatology.org/patients/gout); CPPD established teaching.

guillain-barre-syndrome.name: Guillain-Barré syndrome
guillain-barre-syndrome.scope: Ascending symmetric flaccid paralysis, hyporeflexia, autonomic instability, preceding infection (Campylobacter jejuni), albuminocytologic dissociation, IVIG or plasma exchange
guillain-barre-syndrome.core: Rapidly progressive symmetric weakness with reduced reflexes after infection suggests immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy; respiratory and autonomic monitoring are immediate priorities.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Campylobacter gastroenteritis, respiratory viral infection, CMV; typically 1–3 weeks earlier
Rare postvaccination association; infection poses greater risk than routine vaccination

rows.label: Clues
items: Leg weakness ascends over days, paresthesias, back/radicular pain, bilateral facial weakness
★ **Areflexia with flaccid weakness**; sensory complaints usually exceed objective sensory loss
★ **BP swings, arrhythmias, urinary retention**, bulbar dysfunction indicate severe disease
Miller Fisher variant: ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia; maximal weakness usually within 4 weeks

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Molecular mimicry triggers antibodies against peripheral nerve components
Demyelinating conduction block most common in US; axonal variants also occur

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Serial **forced vital capacity and inspiratory force**; pulse oximetry misses early ventilatory weakness
LP: **↑protein with few cells**; CSF may be normal during first week
Nerve conduction studies: slowing/conduction block or axonal loss; normal early studies do not exclude
Marked CSF pleocytosis, sensory level, or early sphincter dysfunction → reconsider mimics

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Admit for telemetry, swallowing evaluation, frequent strength and breathing assessments
Declining FVC, often <20 mL/kg, weak cough/bulbar dysfunction → **early elective intubation**
★ **IVIG or plasma exchange** for nonambulatory, rapidly progressive, or significant respiratory/bulbar disease
Do not combine routinely; **glucocorticoids do not help**
DVT prophylaxis, pressure care, nutrition, pain control, PT; avoid succinylcholine because hyperkalemia risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Respiratory failure, aspiration, lethal dysautonomia, VTE, pressure injuries
Residual weakness, neuropathic pain, prolonged fatigue; recovery usually spans months

rows.label: Prevention
items: No established primary prophylaxis; early rehabilitation and immobilization precautions reduce secondary injury
Monitor for treatment-related fluctuations; progression beyond 8 weeks raises concern for CIDP

rows.label: Mimics
items: Transverse myelitis: sensory level, early bladder dysfunction, eventual hyperreflexia
Myasthenia gravis: fatigable ocular/bulbar weakness, normal reflexes and sensation
Botulism: descending paralysis, pupillary dysfunction, preserved sensorium

guillain-barre-syndrome.evidence: Not checked online; established neurology teaching.

hearing-loss.name: Hearing loss
hearing-loss.scope: Conductive vs sensorineural hearing loss, Weber and Rinne tests, presbycusis, ototoxicity (cisplatin, aminoglycosides, loop diuretics), noise-induced, Meniere disease, acoustic neuroma
hearing-loss.core: Distinguish impaired sound conduction from cochlear/nerve dysfunction; sudden sensorineural loss requires urgent treatment rather than observation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Aging, occupational/recreational noise, cerumen, chronic middle-ear disease
★ Ototoxins: **cisplatin, aminoglycosides, loop diuretics**; risk increases with renal impairment and combined exposure

rows.label: Clues
items: Presbycusis: bilateral high-frequency loss, difficulty understanding speech amid background noise
Noise injury: high-frequency audiometric notch; tinnitus common
Ménière: episodic vertigo, fluctuating low-frequency loss, tinnitus, aural fullness
★ **Unilateral progressive loss + poor speech discrimination** → vestibular schwannoma; imbalance may accompany

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Conductive: external/middle-ear transmission impaired; sensorineural: cochlea or auditory nerve damaged
Chronic noise/aging preferentially damages basal cochlear hair cells; Ménière involves endolymphatic hydrops

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Otoscopy → tuning forks → formal audiometry**, including air/bone thresholds and speech testing
Tympanometry evaluates middle-ear mechanics; asymmetric sensorineural loss → MRI internal auditory canals
Sudden loss: ≥30 dB across ≥3 contiguous frequencies within 72 hours; urgent audiogram/ENT
Do not attribute sudden unilateral deficit to cerumen without confirming resolution after removal

rows.label: Tx
items: Remove cerumen, treat effusion/infection or structural cause; persistent conductive disease → ENT
★ Sudden sensorineural loss → **corticosteroids promptly**, within 2 weeks; intratympanic route possible
Chronic bilateral deficit → hearing aids, communication strategies; severe refractory loss → cochlear implant evaluation
Ménière: sodium moderation, selected diuretic; short-term vestibular suppressant during attacks
Vestibular schwannoma: observation, stereotactic radiation, or surgery according to tumor size and symptoms

rows.label: Complications
items: Communication barriers, social isolation, depression, impaired safety awareness
Ototoxicity can be permanent; vestibular injury can cause imbalance and falls

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hearing protection, safe listening levels, baseline/serial audiometry with ototoxic drugs

rows.label: Mimics
items: Auditory processing/cognitive disorder: difficulty understanding despite relatively preserved peripheral thresholds
BPPV: brief positional vertigo without hearing loss

heart-failure.name: Heart failure
heart-failure.scope: HFrEF, HFpEF, acute decompensated heart failure, cardiogenic flash pulmonary edema, guideline-directed medical therapy, neurohormonal activation (RAAS, ADH-mediated hyponatremia)
heart-failure.core: Inadequate cardiac output or elevated filling pressures → pulmonary or systemic congestion, even with a normal ejection fraction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: CAD, hypertension, valvular disease, cardiomyopathy, alcohol, cardiotoxic chemotherapy
Decompensation triggers: ischemia, infection, arrhythmia, missed diuretics, NSAIDs

rows.label: Clues
items: Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, elevated JVP, crackles, dependent edema
S3 suggests volume overload; S4 suggests stiff ventricle
★ **Flash edema**: abrupt respiratory distress, severe hypertension, pink frothy sputum

rows.label: Pathophys
items: RAAS/sympathetic activation → vasoconstriction, sodium retention, adverse remodeling
Nonosmotic **ADH** release → dilutional hyponatremia; marker of advanced disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Echocardiography**: EF, valves, wall motion; ECG, CXR, BNP support diagnosis
Low BNP argues against HF; obesity lowers BNP, renal dysfunction raises it
Identify precipitant: troponin, CBC, electrolytes, creatinine; evaluate ischemic cause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute congestion → **IV furosemide**; hypoxemia → oxygen; respiratory distress → noninvasive ventilation
★ Hypertensive pulmonary edema → **IV nitroglycerin**; shock → norepinephrine ± dobutamine, urgent cause correction
Start beta-blocker only when compensated; ACE inhibitor → ARNI requires 36-hour washout
MRA requires eGFR >30, K <5; persistent EF ≤35% despite GDMT → consider ICD

rows.label: Complications
items: Cardiorenal syndrome, ventricular arrhythmia, sudden death, hepatic congestion
Diuresis → hypokalemia; RAAS blockade → hyperkalemia, renal dysfunction; monitor creatinine/K

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Daily weights, sodium moderation, adherence; **continue GDMT after EF recovery**
Treat hypertension, CAD, AF; smoking cessation, exercise, influenza/pneumococcal vaccination

rows.label: Mimics
items: COPD: obstructive spirometry, hyperinflation
Nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia
PE: pleuritic pain, thrombotic risk, RV strain

heart-failure.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACC HFrEF 2024](https://www.acc.org/Latest-in-Cardiology/ten-points-to-remember/2024/03/06/19/22/2024-acc-expert-consensus-hfref); other points established teaching.

humeral-fractures.name: Humeral fractures
humeral-fractures.scope: Proximal humerus fracture (axillary nerve), humeral shaft fracture (radial nerve, wrist drop), neurologic assessment, coaptation splint, functional brace, surgical fixation indications
humeral-fractures.core: Humeral fracture management depends on location, displacement, and neurovascular injury; document nerve function before and after manipulation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older adults with osteoporosis: low-energy proximal fractures; younger adults: high-energy trauma
Shaft injuries from direct blow, twisting, falls; consider malignancy with minimal-trauma shaft fracture

rows.label: Clues
items: Upper-arm pain, swelling, ecchymosis, deformity; reduced shoulder/elbow motion
★ Proximal/surgical neck injury → **axillary nerve**: lateral shoulder numbness, impaired deltoid function
★ Shaft injury → **radial nerve**: wrist/finger extension weakness, dorsal first-web-space sensory loss
Cold pulseless hand, expanding hematoma, severe stretch pain → urgent vascular/compartment evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Axillary nerve wraps around surgical neck; radial nerve travels along the spiral groove
Closed-fracture radial palsy often reflects neurapraxia and recovers without immediate exploration

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **AP/lateral humerus radiographs including shoulder and elbow**; dedicated joint views when involved
Check pulses, capillary refill, motor/sensory function of radial, median, ulnar, and axillary nerves
Repeat examination after reduction/splinting; CT for complex proximal/articular fracture planning
Open wound near fracture → evaluate as open fracture even if bone not visible

rows.label: Tx
items: Analgesia, immobilization, ice; open injury → IV cefazolin, tetanus protection, urgent irrigation/debridement
★ Most closed shaft fractures → **coaptation splint**, then functional brace after swelling subsides
Minimally displaced proximal fracture → sling, early supervised range of motion to limit stiffness
Displaced complex proximal patterns → fixation or selected arthroplasty depending on age and reconstructability
★ Surgery: **open fracture, vascular injury, floating elbow**, unacceptable alignment, failed bracing/nonunion

rows.label: Complications
items: Radial nerve palsy, malunion/nonunion; proximal injuries: avascular necrosis, shoulder stiffness
Secondary/new palsy after reduction or penetrating injury → urgent specialist reassessment, possible exploration

rows.label: Prevention
items: Fall reduction, osteoporosis evaluation after fragility fracture; rehabilitation preserves joint motion
No prolonged unmonitored sling use; regular alignment and neurovascular follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Shoulder dislocation: altered contour and displaced humeral head on joint views
Rotator cuff tear: weakness without fracture, especially persistent after healing

humeral-fractures.evidence: Not checked online; established orthopedic teaching.

hypercalcemia.name: Hypercalcemia
hypercalcemia.scope: Primary hyperparathyroidism, malignancy-associated hypercalcemia, milk-alkali syndrome, IV saline resuscitation, calcitonin, bisphosphonates
hypercalcemia.core: Elevated calcium causes stones, constipation, polyuria, weakness, and neuropsychiatric changes; PTH distinguishes hormone-driven disease from other causes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Parathyroid adenoma/hyperplasia, malignancy, prolonged immobilization
Thiazides, lithium, excess vitamin D or calcium/absorbable alkali, granulomatous disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Dehydration, nausea, abdominal pain, reduced reflexes; ECG may show shortened QT
★ **Calcium >14 mg/dL**, confusion, arrhythmia, or severe volume depletion → urgent treatment
Primary hyperparathyroidism often asymptomatic; malignancy-associated disease tends to progress rapidly

rows.label: Pathophys
items: PTH promotes bone resorption and renal calcium retention while increasing phosphate excretion
Hypercalcemia impairs renal concentration → dehydration, reduced calcium clearance, self-reinforcing elevation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Confirm with repeat total/albumin-adjusted or **ionized calcium**, especially with altered proteins or critical illness
★ **Intact PTH first**; elevated or inappropriately normal → PTH-dependent
Suppressed PTH → PTHrP, vitamin D metabolites, malignancy/myeloma evaluation guided by context
Primary disease versus FHH → urine calcium; clearance ratio <0.01 favors FHH, with overlap
Parathyroid imaging localizes before surgery; never establishes biochemical diagnosis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe/symptomatic → **IV isotonic saline**, then calcitonin for rapid temporary lowering
★ **IV zoledronic acid** for sustained malignancy control; denosumab if severe renal limitations/refractory disease
Calcitriol-mediated disease → glucocorticoids; dialysis for refractory life-threatening elevation or inability to hydrate
Primary disease: surgery for symptoms, age <50, calcium >1 above ULN, osteoporosis/fracture, stones, eGFR <60
Stop causative supplements/drugs; loop diuretic only for fluid overload, not routine calcium elimination

rows.label: Complications
items: Nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, AKI, osteoporosis/fractures, pancreatitis
Calcitonin tachyphylaxis after 48–72 hours; antiresorptives can cause hypocalcemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hydration, avoid excess calcium/alkali; monitor calcium, renal function, and bone density when observing primary disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: FHH: lifelong mild elevation, family history, hypocalciuria; surgery ineffective
Pseudohypercalcemia: high protein-bound calcium but normal ionized fraction

hypercalcemia.evidence: Not checked online; established calcium evaluation and emergency management.

hyperglycemic-crises.name: Hyperglycemic crises
hyperglycemic-crises.core: Insulin-deficient diabetes with osmotic diuresis: rapid acidotic illness or slowly progressive hyperosmolar encephalopathy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Infection, missed insulin, pump failure, MI; DKA often type 1, HHS often older type 2
Euglycemic triggers: **SGLT2 inhibitors**, pregnancy, fasting

rows.label: Clues
items: Polyuria, thirst, weight loss, dry mucosa, tachycardia
DKA: abdominal pain, vomiting, **Kussmaul breathing**; HHS: profound dehydration, focal deficits
★ Severe: **hypotension, stupor**, or coma → ICU

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Insulin deficit + counterregulatory hormones → lipolysis, ketogenesis; residual insulin in HHS limits ketosis
Total-body K depleted despite initially normal/high serum K

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Glucose, electrolytes, venous pH, β-hydroxybutyrate**, osmolality; ECG + trigger evaluation
Effective osmolality = 2 × Na + glucose/18; glucose in mg/dL
★ HHS: **effective osmolality >300 OR total >320 mOsm/kg**; substantial ketosis/acidosis → mixed DKA/HHS
DKA resolution: ketones <0.6 mmol/L AND (pH ≥7.3 OR HCO₃ ≥18); urine ketones/anion gap misleading

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **IV isotonic crystalloid → K correction → IV regular insulin**; K <3.5 mmol/L → delay insulin
Replace K when <5 mmol/L; glucose checks every 1–2 h, electrolytes/pH/ketones every 4 h
★ Add **dextrose** below glucose 250; euglycemic presentation → immediately; continue insulin until crisis resolves
SC basal insulin overlaps infusion 1–2 h; bicarbonate only consider pH <7.0; HHS: slower osmolar correction

rows.label: Complications
items: AKI, thrombosis; treatment: hypoglycemia, hypokalemic arrhythmias, cerebral edema, hyperchloremic acidosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Sick-day fluids/ketone checks; continue basal insulin; ensure supplies and early follow-up
Hold SGLT2 inhibitors during acute illness and before surgery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Alcoholic ketoacidosis: binge then poor intake; usually no diabetes
Starvation ketosis: usually milder acidosis, no marked hyperglycemia
Toxic alcohols: osmolar gap, exposure; absent substantial ketonemia

table.title: Biochemistry; ketones and HCO₃ in mmol/L

hyperthyroidism.name: Hyperthyroidism and thyrotoxicosis
hyperthyroidism.scope: Graves disease, toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma, subacute thyroiditis, thyroid storm, beta-blockers, thionamides, radioactive iodine
hyperthyroidism.core: Excess circulating thyroid hormone → heat intolerance, weight loss despite appetite, tremor, and tachycardia; hormone overproduction differs from destructive release.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune history, female sex; older age favors autonomous nodules
Iodine load, amiodarone, exogenous thyroid hormone; infection/surgery can precipitate storm

rows.label: Clues
items: Hyperreflexia, frequent stools, proximal weakness, widened pulse pressure; older adults may have apathetic presentation
★ **Thyroid storm**: fever, delirium, severe tachyarrhythmia, vomiting, heart failure; clinical diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Increased tissue metabolic activity and beta-adrenergic sensitivity explain systemic manifestations
Thionamides block thyroid peroxidase; PTU also reduces peripheral T4 → T3 conversion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TSH first → free T4**, total T3 if T4 normal; suppressed TSH with elevated hormones
TRAb establishes Graves; uncertain cause → radioactive iodine uptake, except pregnancy/lactation
Low uptake: thyroiditis/exogenous hormone; low thyroglobulin supports exogenous ingestion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptom control: **propranolol**; caution in asthma or decompensated HF
★ Storm → ICU, cooling/fluids, beta-blockade if tolerated, **PTU → iodine ≥1 hour later**, hydrocortisone
Radioiodine contraindicated during pregnancy/lactation; significant active orbitopathy favors another definitive treatment
Compression/suspicious nodule → thyroidectomy after control; pregnancy: first-trimester PTU, later methimazole

rows.label: Complications
items: AF, embolism, osteoporosis, cardiomyopathy; radioiodine often → hypothyroidism
★ Thionamides: **fever/sore throat → stop drug, urgent CBC**; PTU → severe hepatotoxicity

rows.label: Prevention
items: Monitor free T4 early during treatment; TSH recovery lags
Smoking cessation for orbitopathy; definitive treatment before planned pregnancy when feasible

rows.label: Mimics
items: Panic disorder: episodic symptoms without thyroid biochemical abnormalities
Pheochromocytoma: paroxysmal headache, sweating, severe hypertension
Menopause: hot flashes with menstrual transition, normal thyroid testing

table.title: Etiology determines treatment
rows: Diffuse uptake; bruit, orbitopathy, pretibial myxedema
One hot nodule, suppressed surrounding tissue
NSAID; prednisone if severe; no thionamides

hypothyroidism.name: Hypothyroidism
hypothyroidism.scope: Hashimoto thyroiditis, subclinical hypothyroidism, myxedema coma, autoimmune associations, levothyroxine dosing, TSH monitoring
hypothyroidism.core: Insufficient thyroid hormone slows metabolism, causing fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, and delayed reflex relaxation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hashimoto autoimmunity, thyroid surgery/radioiodine, iodine deficiency/excess
Lithium, amiodarone, postpartum thyroiditis; pituitary surgery/radiation or mass

rows.label: Clues
items: Weight gain, bradycardia, hoarseness, heavy menses, hyperlipidemia; hyponatremia in severe disease
★ **Hypothermia, altered mentation, hypoventilation, hypotension** → myxedema coma
Autoimmune clustering: type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia, adrenal insufficiency, celiac disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced hormone activity lowers thermogenesis and cardiac output; glycosaminoglycan deposition produces nonpitting edema
Hashimoto: lymphocytic destruction; anti-TPO antibodies support autoimmune cause

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TSH and free T4** establish hormone deficiency and localize the level of dysfunction
Positive anti-TPO predicts progression from subclinical disease; ultrasound unnecessary without nodule/goiter concern
Recheck mild isolated TSH elevation after transient illness resolves; exclude medication interference

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Levothyroxine**; healthy young adult approximately 1.6 mcg/kg/day; older/CAD start 12.5–25 mcg/day
Take fasting; separate calcium/iron; reassess TSH about 6–8 weeks after changes
Central disease: titrate using free T4; evaluate/replace cortisol before thyroid hormone
Subclinical: generally treat TSH ≥10; consider symptoms, antibodies, pregnancy at lower values
★ Myxedema: **IV levothyroxine + IV hydrocortisone**, airway support, cautious fluids/passive warming; treat trigger

rows.label: Complications
items: Dyslipidemia, infertility, pericardial effusion, neuropathy; severe disease → respiratory failure
Excess replacement → AF, angina, bone loss; rapid correction in CAD can precipitate ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Pregnancy: early **TSH monitoring**, usually increase existing replacement promptly; use pregnancy-specific targets
Monitor stable replacement at least annually; address adherence/absorption before escalating doses

rows.label: Mimics
items: Depression: mood symptoms without thyroid biochemical pattern
Euthyroid sick syndrome: acute systemic illness, often low T3; avoid routine hormone replacement

hypothyroidism.evidence: Not checked online; established thyroid replacement and endocrine emergency teaching.

iga-vasculitis.name: IgA vasculitis
iga-vasculitis.scope: Palpable purpura, arthritis/arthralgias, abdominal pain, intussusception, renal involvement (hematuria, proteinuria, IgA nephropathy), urinalysis monitoring
iga-vasculitis.core: A child with dependent palpable purpura, joint pain, abdominal pain, and renal findings has IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Usually children age 3–15 years, often following upper respiratory infection
Adults can develop disease with greater renal morbidity; medications/infections may precede episodes

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Nonthrombocytopenic purpura** over buttocks and lower legs; lesions may begin as urticaria
Ankle/knee arthralgia or arthritis, colicky pain, GI bleeding; abdominal symptoms can precede rash
Microscopic hematuria/proteinuria may be silent; scrotal pain/swelling can occur
★ **Severe episodic pain, vomiting, bloody stool** → evaluate intussusception or bowel ischemia

rows.label: Pathophys
items: IgA-containing immune complexes deposit in small vessels and renal mesangium
Vascular inflammation causes skin hemorrhage, bowel-wall edema, joint symptoms, and glomerular injury

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Classic presentation → **clinical diagnosis**; CBC/platelets, creatinine, urinalysis, BP at baseline
Quantify urine protein if present; complement generally normal, unlike many immune-complex nephritides
Atypical rash → skin biopsy with leukocytoclastic vasculitis and IgA deposition
Persistent substantial proteinuria, hypertension, or impaired kidney function → nephrology, possible renal biopsy
Acute concerning abdominal symptoms → **ultrasound** for intussusception; location often small bowel

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Most cases → **hydration, rest, acetaminophen**; NSAIDs only without renal impairment/GI bleeding
Severe abdominal/joint symptoms → glucocorticoids after excluding surgical complication
Renal disease: BP/proteinuria control with ACE inhibitor/ARB; severe nephritis → biopsy-directed immunosuppression
Intussusception, ischemia, or perforation → urgent pediatric surgical consultation

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent rash, GI hemorrhage, intussusception; nephritic/nephrotic syndrome, CKD
Long-term prognosis mainly follows renal involvement rather than rash severity

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Serial urinalysis and BP for at least 6 months**, longer with abnormalities
Steroids relieve symptoms but **do not reliably prevent nephritis**; counsel on renal warning signs

rows.label: Mimics
items: ITP: low platelets, mucosal bleeding, no vasculitic joint/renal syndrome
Meningococcemia: toxic febrile illness, rapidly progressive purpura, shock
Isolated IgA nephropathy: renal findings without systemic purpura or abdominal disease

iga-vasculitis.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric rheumatology/nephrology teaching.

impetigo.name: Impetigo
impetigo.scope: Nonbullous impetigo (honey-colored crusts), bullous impetigo, Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, topical mupirocin, oral cephalexin, poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis risk
impetigo.core: Contagious superficial bacterial infection causes crusted erosions or fragile blisters, usually in children; lesion extent determines topical versus oral treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Preschool age, warm humid weather, crowding, close contact, shared towels
Skin-barrier disruption from eczema, insect bites, minor trauma, scabies; nasal staphylococcal carriage

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Nonbullous: vesicles/pustules rupture → **honey-colored crusts**, often around nose/mouth
★ Bullous: **flaccid superficial bullae**, collarette scale; intertriginous/truncal distribution common
Usually localized with little systemic illness; high fever, toxicity, diffuse tenderness require broader evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Nonbullous disease: S aureus and/or group A streptococci infect superficial epidermis
Bullous disease: staphylococcal exfoliative toxin cleaves desmoglein 1; bacterial growth remains localized

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical lesions → **clinical diagnosis**; no routine blood tests
Culture exudate when recurrent, extensive, treatment-resistant, outbreak-associated, or MRSA suspected
Deep punched-out crusted ulcer → ecthyma, extending into dermis; consider oral treatment

rows.label: Tx
items: Gently cleanse with soap/water, soften crusts; cover lesions and trim nails
★ Few localized lesions → **topical mupirocin for 5 days**
★ Numerous lesions, outbreaks, ecthyma → **oral cephalexin or dicloxacillin for 7 days**
Suspected/confirmed MRSA → culture-directed clindamycin, doxycycline, or TMP-SMX; account for age and streptococcal coverage
Streptococci alone on culture → oral penicillin; reassess spread or failure to improve

rows.label: Complications
items: Cellulitis, lymphangitis, deeper ulceration with scarring; systemic infection uncommon
**Poststreptococcal GN** can follow skin infection; antibiotics do not reliably prevent it
Acute rheumatic fever classically follows streptococcal pharyngitis rather than uncomplicated impetigo

rows.label: Prevention
items: Handwashing, separate towels, avoid scratching, treat underlying eczema/scabies
Avoid contact sports while contagious; repeated infections may prompt household/colonization assessment

rows.label: Mimics
items: HSV: grouped painful vesicles, recurrent distribution; eczema herpeticum: monomorphic punched-out erosions
Contact dermatitis: prominent itch, exposure-shaped rash, no bacterial crust initially
Staphylococcal scalded skin: diffuse tender peeling, systemic toxin effect, often sterile bullae

infective-endocarditis.name: Infective endocarditis
infective-endocarditis.scope: Native and prosthetic valve endocarditis, Duke criteria, prophylaxis, IV drug use endocarditis, blood culture diagnostic criteria
infective-endocarditis.core: Persistent bacteremia with valve infection causes systemic emboli, valve destruction, and immune-complex injury.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prosthetic valve, prior endocarditis, congenital valve abnormality, intracardiac device
Injection drug use → tricuspid involvement; healthcare exposure, indwelling vascular access

rows.label: Clues
items: Fever, new regurgitant murmur, embolic stroke, splenic infarct, hematuria
Janeway lesions painless; Osler nodes painful; splinter hemorrhages nonspecific
★ **New conduction block** → periannular abscess; right-sided disease → septic pulmonary emboli

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Endothelial injury → platelet-fibrin nidus → microbial adherence and vegetation
Immune complexes → glomerulonephritis; infected fragments disseminate through downstream circulation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Three blood-culture sets before antibiotics**; separate peripheral draws unless resuscitation would be delayed
Major microbiology: **typical organism in ≥2 culture sets**, nontypical in ≥3; specialized serology/PCR also qualifies
★ **TTE → TEE** if prosthesis/high suspicion; major imaging: vegetation, abscess, perforation, new significant regurgitation
Definite clinical Duke: 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria
Minor: predisposition, fever, vascular phenomena, immunologic phenomena, nondiagnostic microbiology

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Empiric **IV vancomycin + cefepime** for acutely ill/healthcare-associated cases; tailor to cultures and setting
MSSA → nafcillin/oxacillin or cefazolin; susceptible viridans streptococci → ceftriaxone
Prolonged pathogen-directed IV antibiotics; prosthetic infections need specialist regimen and early surgical evaluation
Surgery: heart failure, abscess, persistent bacteremia, fungal infection, or selected recurrent/large embolizing vegetations

rows.label: Complications
items: Acute regurgitation, heart failure, mycotic aneurysm, metastatic infection
Antibiotic nephrotoxicity, line infection; hemorrhage into embolic cerebral lesions

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Dental **amoxicillin** for prosthetic valve/material, previous IE, selected cyanotic/residual CHD, transplant valvulopathy
Good oral hygiene, sterile access; no routine prophylaxis for GI/GU procedures or isolated MVP

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis: cancer/autoimmune disease, sterile cultures
Atrial myxoma: positional obstruction, intracavitary mass; vasculitis: no infected vegetation

inflammatory-myopathies.name: Inflammatory myopathies
inflammatory-myopathies.scope: Polymyositis, dermatomyositis, inclusion body myositis, elevated creatine kinase, autoantibodies (anti-Jo-1, anti-Mi-2), muscle biopsy, malignancy screening, systemic corticosteroids
inflammatory-myopathies.core: Objective muscle weakness with elevated muscle enzymes suggests myopathy; distribution, skin findings, and biopsy distinguish treatable inflammation from inclusion body disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune predisposition; adult dermatomyositis associated with occult malignancy
Inclusion body myositis: usually men >50 years; review statin and other myotoxic exposures

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Difficulty rising or lifting arms**, neck flexor weakness; sensation generally preserved
Dysphagia, aspiration, dyspnea warrant evaluation for bulbar/respiratory weakness and interstitial lung disease
Dermatomyositis can have characteristic rash before significant muscle weakness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Polymyositis: T-cell-mediated endomysial injury; dermatomyositis: complement-associated microvascular injury
Inclusion body disease combines inflammatory and degenerative pathology, explaining poor immunosuppressive response

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CK, aldolase, AST/ALT**, TSH; muscle can explain transaminase elevation without primary liver disease
MRI identifies edema and guides **muscle biopsy**; EMG supports a myopathic pattern
★ **Anti-Jo-1**: antisynthetase syndrome with ILD, arthritis, mechanic's hands; **anti-Mi-2**: classic dermatomyositis
Check swallowing and lung function when symptomatic; exclude inherited, endocrine, and drug-induced myopathies

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Polymyositis/dermatomyositis → **systemic glucocorticoids + steroid-sparing agent**, such as methotrexate or azathioprine
Severe/refractory disease or dysphagia → IVIG or other specialist-directed immunomodulation
Inclusion body: PT/OT, mobility aids, swallowing support; immunosuppression usually ineffective
Dermatomyositis rash: sun protection and topical agents; rehabilitation without prolonged immobilization

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, respiratory failure, ILD, myocarditis; juvenile dermatomyositis can cause calcinosis
Steroid myopathy causes new weakness with normal CK; treatment also increases infection and fracture risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Adult dermatomyositis → **age-based plus risk-based malignancy evaluation**, especially near diagnosis
Bone protection, immunizations, infection prophylaxis according to immunosuppressive intensity; monitor strength and CK

rows.label: Mimics
items: Polymyalgia rheumatica: pain/stiffness without true weakness or ↑CK
Myasthenia: fatigability, ocular symptoms, normal CK; ALS: mixed UMN/LMN signs

table.title: Distribution and biopsy
rows: Heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, shawl erythema

interstitial-lung-disease.name: Interstitial lung disease
interstitial-lung-disease.scope: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, sarcoidosis, pneumoconioses, restrictive PFTs (reduced DLCO, normal/high FEV1/FVC), high-resolution CT
interstitial-lung-disease.core: Progressive exertional dyspnea, dry cough, and inspiratory crackles suggest diffuse parenchymal lung disease; HRCT patterns and exposure history identify the cause.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age >60 and smoking: IPF; autoimmune disease; familial fibrosis
Amiodarone, bleomycin, nitrofurantoin; occupational silica/coal/asbestos, organic antigens; prior thoracic radiation

rows.label: Clues
items: Fine basal Velcro crackles, exertional desaturation, later clubbing; systemic rheumatic features can reveal cause
Sarcoidosis: bilateral hilar adenopathy, uveitis, erythema nodosum, sometimes hypercalcemia
Rapidly worsening oxygenation → infection, embolism, edema, or acute exacerbation evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Alveolar/interstitial injury and aberrant repair reduce lung compliance and gas-transfer capacity
Granulomatous inflammation or fibrogenic dust responses produce distinct imaging distributions

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **HRCT + full PFTs** after chest radiograph; obtain detailed drug, occupation, hobby, autoimmune history
★ **↓TLC, ↓DLCO, normal/↑FEV1/FVC** support restriction; low FVC alone is insufficient
UIP: basal subpleural reticulation, traction bronchiectasis, honeycombing; exclude known causes before labeling IPF
Autoantibodies when connective-tissue disease suspected; BAL/biopsy selected through multidisciplinary review
Typical UIP without secondary cause may avoid surgical biopsy; assess exertional oxygen needs

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Remove offending exposure/drug**, pulmonary rehabilitation, oxygen for hypoxemia; treat identified cause
★ IPF: **nintedanib or pirfenidone** slows decline; no routine chronic prednisone-based immunosuppression
Inflammatory sarcoid/autoimmune disease: selected steroids or steroid-sparing agents; mild sarcoid may need observation
Progressive fibrotic non-IPF disease → nintedanib consideration; advanced disease → early transplant evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, respiratory failure, exacerbations; asbestos raises lung cancer/mesothelioma risk
Silicosis increases TB susceptibility; antifibrotics can cause GI adverse effects and liver injury

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, respiratory immunizations, occupational dust controls, medication monitoring; follow FVC/DLCO trends

rows.label: Mimics
items: Heart failure: congestion/cardiomegaly, volume response; emphysema: obstruction with hyperinflation
Neuromuscular restriction: low volumes with relatively preserved diffusion capacity

table.title: Imaging clues to etiology
rows: Centrilobular nodules, mosaic attenuation, air trapping

iron-toxicity.name: Iron toxicity
iron-toxicity.scope: Acute iron poisoning, GI phase, metabolic acidosis, shock, radiopaque pills on abdominal x-ray, deferoxamine chelation, hemochromatosis contrast
iron-toxicity.core: Iron overdose causes corrosive GI injury followed by systemic mitochondrial toxicity; an apparent recovery period can precede shock and liver failure.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Toddler ingestion of prenatal/iron tablets; intentional overdose in adolescents/adults
Toxicity depends on **elemental iron**, not total salt weight; >60 mg/kg can cause severe toxicity

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ First hours: **abdominal pain, vomiting, bloody diarrhea**; severe exposure can rapidly cause circulatory collapse
★ **High-anion-gap acidosis, shock**, lethargy, hyperglycemia signal systemic injury
Temporary symptom improvement does not establish safety; hepatotoxicity may emerge over subsequent days

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Unbound iron generates free radicals, disrupts oxidative phosphorylation, and damages vascular/hepatic tissue
Local GI corrosive injury causes fluid loss; capillary leak and myocardial dysfunction worsen hypotension

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Serum iron at 4–6 hours**, repeat for sustained-release ingestion or rising levels
Late low concentration may reflect tissue redistribution, not absence of toxicity
Abdominal x-ray can show **radiopaque tablets**; negative study does not exclude liquid or dissolved iron
Blood gas, lactate, electrolytes/anion gap, glucose, liver tests, INR; serum ferritin not acute severity marker

rows.label: Tx
items: ABCs, IV crystalloid, glucose/electrolyte correction, vasopressors if needed; contact poison control
★ **IV deferoxamine** for shock, acidosis, severe GI/systemic toxicity, or serum iron >500 µg/dL
Whole-bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol for substantial retained tablets when stable and airway protected
★ **Activated charcoal does not bind iron**; no induced emesis, avoid irrigation with ileus/obstruction/instability
Admit symptomatic/high-risk patients for serial assessment; fulminant hepatic failure → transplant-center evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: GI hemorrhage, shock, hepatic necrosis, coagulopathy; later gastric/pyloric scarring and obstruction
Deferoxamine: hypotension with rapid infusion, lung injury with prolonged use; reddish urine may occur

rows.label: Prevention
items: Locked child-resistant storage; no calling tablets candy; psychiatric assessment after intentional ingestion

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hemochromatosis: chronic accumulation, diabetes/liver disease, ↑transferrin saturation; treat with phlebotomy
Sepsis: shock/acidosis without ingestion history; salicylates: tinnitus, mixed acid-base disorder

ischemic-stroke-and-tia.name: Ischemic stroke and TIA
ischemic-stroke-and-tia.scope: TIA (including amaurosis fugax), ischemic stroke, acute management (tPA, thrombectomy), secondary prevention, risk factors
ischemic-stroke-and-tia.core: Abrupt focal neurologic loss from cerebral ischemia; transient monocular blindness localizes to the ipsilateral carotid circulation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hypertension, smoking, diabetes, dyslipidemia, carotid atherosclerosis
Atrial fibrillation, recent MI, endocarditis, arterial dissection

rows.label: Clues
items: Aphasia or neglect suggests cortical involvement; crossed cranial-nerve/limb findings suggest brainstem disease
★ **Last known well** establishes treatment timing; symptom discovery time may differ
TIA: resolved deficit without acute infarction; urgent evaluation despite normal examination

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Thromboembolism or small-vessel occlusion → infarct core surrounded by salvageable penumbra
Reperfusion preserves threatened tissue but increases hemorrhagic transformation risk

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Fingerstick glucose + **noncontrast head CT** first; normal early CT does not exclude ischemia
CTA head/neck for large-vessel occlusion; MRI diffusion for small infarcts or diagnostic uncertainty
ECG, telemetry, carotid imaging; echocardiography for suspected cardiac emboli

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Disabling deficit, eligible ≤4.5 hours → **alteplase or tenecteplase**; imaging-selected extended windows possible
Thrombolysis: BP <185/110 before, <180/105 after; exclude bleeding and significant anticoagulant effect
★ Large-vessel occlusion → **mechanical thrombectomy**, selected cases through 24 hours; do not delay thrombolysis
No reperfusion: generally allow BP ≤220/120; oxygen for hypoxemia; swallow assessment before oral intake
Aspirin after hemorrhage excluded; after thrombolysis, wait 24 hours and repeat imaging

rows.label: Complications
items: Cerebral edema, aspiration, venous thrombosis, seizures, disability

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Minor noncardioembolic stroke/high-risk TIA → short **aspirin + clopidogrel**, then single antiplatelet
AF → oral anticoagulation with timing based on infarct/bleeding risk; high-intensity statin, BP control
Symptomatic carotid stenosis 70–99% → endarterectomy when eligible; selected 50–69% also benefit

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hypoglycemia: deficit reverses with glucose
Migraine aura: spreading positive symptoms; seizure: witnessed convulsion followed by Todd paralysis

kawasaki-disease.name: Kawasaki disease
kawasaki-disease.scope: Diagnostic criteria (CRASH and burn), echocardiography, coronary artery aneurysms, intravenous immunoglobulin, aspirin, refractory disease
kawasaki-disease.core: Persistent fever with mucocutaneous inflammation in a young child suggests Kawasaki disease; early treatment reduces coronary artery injury.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Usually age <5 years; more common in children of East Asian ancestry
Infants, delayed diagnosis, and early coronary abnormalities increase complication risk

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Fever ≥5 days + ≥4 CRASH features**; experienced clinicians may diagnose earlier when classic
C: bilateral nonpurulent conjunctivitis; R: polymorphous rash; A: cervical adenopathy, usually unilateral >1.5 cm
S: oral strawberry tongue/cracked red lips; H: hand/foot erythema/edema → later periungual peeling
Irritability, sterile pyuria, ↑ESR/CRP; thrombocytosis typically after first week, not required initially

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immune-mediated medium-vessel vasculitis preferentially injures coronary arteries
Inflammation weakens arterial walls → dilation/aneurysm, thrombosis, and later stenosis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis + echocardiography** at presentation; normal initial echo does not exclude disease
Prolonged unexplained fever with 2–3 features, especially infant → incomplete-disease inflammatory/echo algorithm
CBC, CRP/ESR, albumin, liver tests, urinalysis support assessment; no single confirmatory laboratory test
Repeat echo at approximately 1–2 and 4–6 weeks; more frequent for coronary abnormalities

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **IVIG + aspirin promptly**, ideally within first 10 days; treat later if ongoing inflammation/coronary disease
Acute anti-inflammatory aspirin → low-dose antiplatelet phase after afebrile; duration follows coronary findings
★ High-risk disease → consider **adjunct glucocorticoids** with initial IVIG through specialist team
Fever ≥36 hours after IVIG → reassess; repeat IVIG, infliximab, or steroids for refractory disease
Large/giant aneurysms → additional anticoagulation with cardiology; manage shock/myocarditis supportively

rows.label: Complications
items: Coronary aneurysm, thrombosis, MI, myocarditis, ventricular dysfunction, valvular regurgitation
IVIG can cause hemolysis; aspirin increases bleeding and Reye risk during influenza/varicella

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ After IVIG, **delay MMR/varicella approximately 11 months**; maintain cardiology follow-up
Annual inactivated influenza vaccination while receiving aspirin; promptly discuss varicella exposure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Adenovirus: exudative conjunctivitis/pharyngitis; scarlet fever: positive streptococcal testing, no coronary involvement
MIS-C: recent SARS-CoV-2, older child, marked GI symptoms/shock, often thrombocytopenia

knee-injuries.name: Knee injuries
knee-injuries.scope: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear, posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) tear, collateral ligaments, meniscal tears, knee dislocation, popliteal artery injury, Ottawa knee rules
knee-injuries.core: Knee trauma assessment starts with neurovascular safety and fracture risk, then uses mechanism, effusion timing, and targeted ligament or meniscal tests.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pivoting/cutting sports, contact trauma, dashboard impact, hyperextension
Older age, osteoporosis, and inability to bear weight increase fracture probability

rows.label: Clues
items: Immediate large effusion suggests hemarthrosis; delayed swelling and catching suggest meniscal injury
★ **Gross deformity or spontaneously reduced dislocation** → popliteal artery injury risk
Cool foot, weak pulses, paresthesia, escalating pain → vascular compromise or compartment syndrome

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Ligament disruption → instability; displaced meniscal fragment → mechanical locking
Knee dislocation may stretch/tear popliteal artery despite restored alignment and initially palpable pulses

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Neurovascular examination before and after reduction**; ABI assesses arterial injury
★ ABI **<0.9 or abnormal pulses → CT angiography**; hard ischemic signs → immediate vascular intervention
Normal ABI/pulses after dislocation → serial vascular checks, not immediate discharge
Ottawa: age ≥55, isolated patellar/fibular-head tenderness, flexion <90°, or inability four-step weight-bearing → radiographs
MRI for soft-tissue injury after fracture evaluation; locked knee → prompt orthopedic assessment

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Dislocation → **urgent reduction**, immobilization, orthopedic/vascular consultation
Initial sprain → ice/compression, analgesia, protected weight bearing then early rehabilitation
Isolated collateral sprain → hinged brace + rehabilitation; many PCL injuries managed nonoperatively
ACL rupture with athletic demands/persistent instability or combined injury → reconstruction discussion
Displaced locked meniscal tear → arthroscopy; degenerative tears without locking usually exercise-based rehabilitation

rows.label: Complications
items: Missed arterial injury → limb loss; peroneal nerve injury → foot drop
Chronic instability, recurrent meniscal injury, posttraumatic osteoarthritis, stiffness

rows.label: Prevention
items: Neuromuscular landing/pivot training, strength and balance rehabilitation before sport return

rows.label: Mimics
items: Patellar dislocation: lateral patellar displacement, often spontaneous reduction
Septic arthritis: atraumatic hot effusion, fever; urgent aspiration

knee-injuries.evidence: Not checked online; established orthopedic trauma and Ottawa knee principles.

low-back-pain.name: Low back pain
low-back-pain.scope: Lumbosacral strain, herniated disk and radiculopathy, spinal stenosis, red flags, imaging indications, conservative management
low-back-pain.core: Most acute low back pain improves with activity and analgesia; neurologic deficits or systemic red flags change the workup.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Heavy lifting, deconditioning, obesity, prolonged sitting
Cancer, immunosuppression, injection drug use, osteoporosis, chronic glucocorticoids increase serious-pathology risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Mechanical pain varies with movement; isolated axial pain without systemic illness favors benign disease
★ **Urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, bilateral weakness** → cauda equina emergency
Fever, weight loss, night pain, trauma, or progressive weakness → targeted urgent evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Paraspinal injury causes localized pain; degenerative narrowing or disk extrusion compresses neural structures

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ No red flags → **no initial imaging**, including routine radiographs
Focused strength, reflex, sensory, gait examination; straight-leg raise supports lower lumbar radiculopathy
★ Suspected infection, malignancy, cord compression → **MRI**; suspected fracture → radiograph or CT
Persistent symptoms despite about 6 weeks' care → MRI if intervention being considered
Suspected spinal infection → ESR/CRP, blood cultures; normal temperature does not exclude infection

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Continue activity**, superficial heat, short NSAID course; avoid prolonged bed rest
Physical rehabilitation for persistent symptoms; avoid routine opioids and systemic steroids
Progressive motor deficit or cauda equina → urgent surgical decompression
Refractory disabling radicular pain → epidural injection or diskectomy after imaging correlation

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic pain, functional limitation, medication dependence
Untreated compression → permanent bladder, bowel, sexual, or motor dysfunction

rows.label: Prevention
items: Core strengthening, regular exercise, ergonomic lifting, weight management
Return to usual tasks gradually; address fear avoidance and workplace barriers

rows.label: Mimics
items: AAA: abdominal pulsatile mass, vascular risk, hypotension
Renal colic: flank-to-groin pain, hematuria; inflammatory back pain: improves with exercise

table.title: Mechanical patterns
rows: Leg pain below knee; cough aggravates

low-back-pain.evidence: Not checked online; established generalist back-pain evaluation.

lung-cancer.name: Lung cancer
lung-cancer.scope: Non-small cell, small cell, paraneoplastic syndromes, Pancoast, screening
lung-cancer.core: Persistent cough, hemoptysis, weight loss, or a suspicious lung lesion requires tissue diagnosis and staging before treatment selection.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, radon, asbestos, occupational carcinogens, prior thoracic radiation; adenocarcinoma also occurs in never-smokers

rows.label: Clues
items: Recurrent focal pneumonia, hoarseness, clubbing, unexplained pleural effusion
★ **Pancoast tumor**: shoulder/ulnar-arm pain + ipsilateral Horner syndrome
SVC obstruction: facial swelling, neck-vein distention; cord compression or airway compromise requires urgent action

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Bronchogenic malignant transformation → local invasion, lymphatic spread, hematogenous metastasis
Ectopic hormone production and immune cross-reactivity cause paraneoplastic syndromes

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspicious finding → **contrast chest CT**; biopsy easiest site that establishes highest stage
Central lesion/nodes → bronchoscopy/EBUS; peripheral lesion → CT-guided biopsy; effusion → cytology
PET/CT for extracranial staging, brain MRI for selected stages/small-cell disease; pulmonary function before resection
Molecular profiling and PD-L1 guide advanced NSCLC treatment; suspicious nodes often require pathologic staging

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Early operable NSCLC → **surgical resection + nodal evaluation**; inoperable localized → stereotactic radiation
Locally advanced NSCLC → combined systemic treatment/radiation ± surgery in selected patients
Metastatic NSCLC → biomarker-directed agents or immunotherapy/chemotherapy
★ Small-cell → **platinum + etoposide**, stage-dependent radiation/immunotherapy; surgery rarely used

rows.label: Complications
items: Brain/bone/adrenal/liver metastases, malignant effusion, thrombosis, respiratory failure
Radiation pneumonitis; checkpoint inhibitors → immune pneumonitis/endocrinopathies

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ USPSTF: **annual low-dose CT**, age 50–80, ≥20 pack-years, current smoking or quit <15 years
Stop after 15 quit-years or limited curative candidacy; **ACS omits quit-time restriction**
Smoking cessation and radon mitigation; chest radiographs do not substitute for screening CT

rows.label: Mimics
items: TB/fungal granuloma: microbiologic evidence; PET uptake not specific for cancer
Hamartoma: fat/popcorn calcification; pneumonia: clinical/radiographic response to antibiotics

lung-cancer.evidence: Screening checked 2026-10-30: [USPSTF 2021](https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/lung-cancer-screening), [ACS 2023 guideline](https://acsjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.3322/caac.21811); treatment: established stage-based framework.

medical-errors-and-patient-safety.name: Medical errors and patient safety
medical-errors-and-patient-safety.scope: Near miss, adverse event, error disclosure, root cause analysis, structured sign-outs and handoffs
medical-errors-and-patient-safety.core: Protect the patient first, disclose errors honestly, and redesign systems to reduce recurrence.

rows.label: Principle
items: Just culture: distinguish human error, risky shortcuts, and reckless conduct
Psychological safety enables reporting; accountability and system improvement can coexist

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **Stabilize and mitigate harm**, notify supervising clinician, preserve relevant clinical information
★ Disclose facts, consequences, **apology**, treatment/prevention plans; update uncertainties
★ Report through institutional safety system; document clinical facts and disclosure in medical record

rows.label: Don't
items: Avoid concealment, altered records, premature blame, or speculation about causation
Do not rely on education alone when workflow permits predictable repeated errors

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Reckless impairment/dangerous conduct → remove from unsafe duties; institutional escalation

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Root cause analysis**: retrospective system investigation; identify multiple contributors
Failure mode and effects analysis: prospective hazard assessment before harm
Handoff: standardized I-PASS/SBAR, pending tasks, contingency plans, receiver synthesis/read-back

medical-errors-and-patient-safety.evidence: Not checked online; established patient-safety terminology and ethical disclosure principles.

normal-and-abnormal-labor.name: Normal and abnormal labor
normal-and-abnormal-labor.scope: Latent vs active first stage, second stage, active phase protraction and arrest (oxytocin, cesarean), false labor (Braxton Hicks), operative vaginal delivery, labor induction
normal-and-abnormal-labor.core: True labor produces progressive cervical change; dystocia management depends on stage, contraction adequacy, fetal status, and descent.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Nulliparity, obesity, fetal macrosomia, malposition, cephalopelvic disproportion, inadequate uterine contractions

rows.label: Clues
items: Assess membrane status, presentation, fetal heart tracing, serial dilation, station, and maternal vital signs
★ Tachysystole: **>5 contractions/10 minutes**, averaged over 30 minutes

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dysfunctional powers, passenger, or passage → delayed dilation or descent

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Active arrest requires ruptured membranes: no change after **4 hours adequate** or 6 hours inadequate contractions
Adequate activity: ≥200 Montevideo units; intrauterine pressure catheter when external assessment insufficient
Prolonged pushing: >3 hours nulliparous, >2 hours multiparous; individualize by descent and fetal status
Failed induction requires ≥12–18 hours oxytocin after ROM; slow latent phase alone does not mandate cesarean

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Protraction with weak contractions → **oxytocin**, amniotomy; established active arrest → cesarean
Tachysystole → stop oxytocin, lateral positioning; persistent fetal compromise → terbutaline, expedited delivery
★ Operative vaginal birth requires full dilation, ruptured membranes, engaged head, known position, skilled operator
Unfavorable cervix → balloon or prostaglandin ripening, then oxytocin; avoid misoprostol after prior cesarean
Avoid vacuum before 34 weeks or with face presentation; failed operative attempt → cesarean

rows.label: Complications
items: Maternal infection, hemorrhage, exhaustion; neonatal hypoxia
Forceps/vacuum → maternal lacerations, neonatal scalp injury; vacuum → subgaleal hemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: Induce for maternal/fetal indications or offer elective induction from 39 weeks; no elective earlier delivery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Braxton Hicks: irregular contractions without cervical change
Obstructed labor: adequate contractions without progress; augmentation cannot correct mechanical obstruction

nutritional-deficiencies.name: Nutritional deficiencies
nutritional-deficiencies.scope: Vegan diet nutrient risks, tea-and-toast diet, vitamin and mineral supplementation, clinical manifestations
nutritional-deficiencies.core: Restricted intake, malabsorption, or increased requirements produce characteristic mucocutaneous, neurologic, hematologic, and skeletal findings; identify the missing nutrient and its cause.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Unsupplemented vegan diet: B12, iron, calcium, vitamin D, iodine, zinc risks
Tea-and-toast diet, alcohol misuse, food insecurity, restrictive eating, institutionalization
Bariatric surgery, pancreatic insufficiency, cholestasis, bowel disease → specific or fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption

rows.label: Clues
items: Poor wound healing, bruising, oral changes, neuropathy, bone pain; mixed deficiencies commonly coexist
★ **Confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia** in malnutrition → thiamine deficiency; complete triad often absent
Night blindness → vitamin A; bleeding with prolonged PT → vitamin K
Dermatitis, diarrhea, cognitive decline → niacin; periorificial/acral dermatitis + alopecia → zinc

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Insufficient cofactors impair energy metabolism, collagen formation, hematopoiesis, or mineralization
Low intake differs from malabsorption: replacement route and lasting supplementation must match the mechanism

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Diet and supplement history**, weight trend, oral/skin/neurologic examination; assess GI disease
CBC/ferritin, B12 ± methylmalonic acid, 25-OH vitamin D chosen by findings; avoid indiscriminate panels
Albumin is altered by inflammation/fluid status; not a stand-alone nutrition diagnostic test
Severely undernourished → baseline phosphate, Mg, K before nutritional rehabilitation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected Wernicke syndrome → **parenteral thiamine promptly**; do not await laboratory confirmation
B12 deficiency with neurologic signs/malabsorption → parenteral replacement; folate only after B12 assessment
Vitamin D/calcium for deficient intake or osteomalacia; iron replacement with evaluation for blood loss
Vitamin C for scurvy; oral balanced nutrition plus cause-directed supplementation and dietitian support
★ Severe malnutrition → **slow refeeding + thiamine**, close phosphate/K/Mg monitoring and replacement

rows.label: Complications
items: Irreversible B12 neurologic injury, fractures, anemia, infection susceptibility
Refeeding → hypophosphatemia, arrhythmia, respiratory failure; excess vitamin A → hepatotoxicity/teratogenicity

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Vegans → **reliable B12 supplementation**; fortified foods, calcium/vitamin D and iodine adequacy
Diversified diet, food access support, lifelong bariatric follow-up; avoid megadose supplementation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Scurvy versus vasculitis: perifollicular hemorrhage/corkscrew hairs, restricted produce intake
Hypothyroidism: fatigue and macrocytosis with elevated TSH

nutritional-deficiencies.evidence: Not checked online; established nutritional deficiency and refeeding principles.

obesity-and-bariatric-surgery.name: Obesity and bariatric surgery
obesity-and-bariatric-surgery.scope: Lifestyle modifications, pharmacotherapy (GLP-1 receptor agonists), indications for bariatric surgery, postoperative nutritional and surgical complications
obesity-and-bariatric-surgery.core: Chronic excess adiposity with metabolic complications; sustained treatment combines nutrition, activity, behavioral support, medications, and sometimes metabolic surgery.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Calorie-dense diet, inactivity, sleep deprivation, genetic susceptibility, food insecurity
Glucocorticoids, antipsychotics, insulin; investigate endocrine causes when examination suggests them

rows.label: Clues
items: BMI ≥30 kg/m²; central adiposity predicts cardiometabolic risk
Screen for hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, sleep apnea, fatty liver, osteoarthritis, depression

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Adipose inflammation and insulin resistance; appetite regulation favors weight regain after weight loss
Bypass and sleeve alter gut signaling and intake; bypass additionally decreases nutrient absorption

rows.label: Dx
items: Weight trajectory, medication review, eating-disorder assessment; A1c, lipids, liver enzymes
★ Postoperative **tachycardia**, fever, abdominal pain → investigate anastomotic leak urgently

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Structured calorie deficit, activity, behavioral follow-up; **5–10% weight loss** improves metabolic disease
Medications: BMI ≥30, or ≥27 with comorbidity; semaglutide or tirzepatide plus lifestyle changes
★ Avoid GLP-1 agents with **MEN 2/medullary thyroid carcinoma** history; avoid weight-loss drugs during pregnancy
★ **Surgical referral** by eligibility below; assess nutritional, operative, psychosocial readiness and lifelong follow-up

rows.label: Complications
items: Early surgery: leak, hemorrhage, VTE; later: stricture, gallstones, internal hernia causing intermittent abdominal pain
Roux-en-Y: dumping after sugary meals, marginal ulcers; iron, B12, calcium, vitamin D deficiencies
Persistent vomiting → thiamine deficiency; give thiamine promptly before carbohydrate loading

rows.label: Prevention
items: Lifelong supplements and nutritional surveillance after surgery; avoid NSAIDs and tobacco after bypass
Small meals, fewer simple sugars for dumping; delay conception during rapid postoperative weight loss

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cushing syndrome: violaceous striae, proximal weakness, easy bruising
Hypothyroidism: cold intolerance, bradycardia; usually modest weight gain

opioid-toxicity.name: Opioid toxicity
opioid-toxicity.scope: Opioid toxidrome, naloxone administration and titration, observation period, precipitated withdrawal
opioid-toxicity.core: Depressed consciousness, slow breathing, and pinpoint pupils after opioid exposure; ventilation takes priority over full awakening.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Fentanyl or heroin exposure, dose escalation, renal dysfunction, long-acting opioids
Alcohol/benzodiazepine co-ingestion; lost tolerance after detoxification, hospitalization, or incarceration

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Bradypnea or apnea** with hypoxemia; reduced bowel sounds, bradycardia, hypotension
Miosis may be absent with severe hypoxia or co-ingestion; needle marks are not required
Pulmonary edema, aspiration, hypothermia, prolonged immobilization may accompany overdose

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mu-receptor activation suppresses medullary ventilatory response to CO2
Naloxone competitively reverses opioid effects but often wears off before the causative opioid

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; bedside glucose, pulse oximetry, capnography; do not await toxicology
Routine urine opioid immunoassay may miss fentanyl, methadone, and oxycodone
ECG for methadone-associated QT prolongation; acetaminophen level with uncertain combination-product ingestion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Open airway, **bag-mask ventilation**, oxygen; intubate if ventilation cannot be maintained
★ **Naloxone** IV titrated to adequate breathing; intranasal/IM route if IV unavailable
Dependent but breathing: start low; apnea: prompt larger/repeated doses without delaying resuscitation
Repeated recurrence → naloxone infusion; persistent coma → evaluate additional causes
Short-acting reversal: observe ≥4 hours after last naloxone; long-acting/recurrent sedation → prolonged monitoring/admission

rows.label: Complications
items: Anoxic brain injury, aspiration pneumonia, rhabdomyolysis, compartment syndrome
Precipitated withdrawal: agitation, vomiting, diarrhea, tachycardia; rare pulmonary edema after reversal

rows.label: Prevention
items: Take-home naloxone, overdose-response training, avoid sedative combinations; offer buprenorphine and addiction follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pontine hemorrhage: focal neurologic findings, no meaningful naloxone response
Clonidine poisoning: marked bradycardia with similar pupils
Sedative overdose: usually normal pupils; incomplete naloxone response

pancreatic-cancer.name: Pancreatic cancer
pancreatic-cancer.scope: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma, painless jaundice, Courvoisier sign, CA 19-9, neuroendocrine tumors (gastrinoma, insulinoma)
pancreatic-cancer.core: Older adult with weight loss and painless obstructive jaundice, or persistent epigastric pain radiating to the back.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, chronic pancreatitis, obesity, increasing age; strong family history, hereditary cancer syndromes
New diabetes with unexplained weight loss can signal occult malignancy

rows.label: Clues
items: Head lesions: dark urine, pale stools, pruritus, nontender palpable gallbladder (**Courvoisier sign**)
Body/tail lesions: late presentation with pain and cachexia; migratory thrombophlebitis may occur

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Ductal adenocarcinoma causes biliary obstruction, perineural invasion, and early metastatic spread
Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors arise from endocrine cells; may be functional or incidental

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pancreatic-protocol CT** for mass, vessels, metastases; ultrasound may initially show biliary dilation
EUS biopsy before systemic treatment/uncertain diagnosis; not mandatory before straightforward resection
★ **CA 19-9** monitors disease; neither screening nor definitive diagnosis; obstruction can falsely elevate
Resectability depends on metastases and major vascular involvement; MRI clarifies indeterminate liver lesions

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Resectable head tumor → **Whipple**; body/tail tumor → distal pancreatectomy; add systemic chemotherapy
Borderline resectable → neoadjuvant treatment; metastatic → systemic treatment and palliation
★ Cholangitis → **urgent ERCP**; unresectable symptomatic jaundice → biliary stent
Analgesia, pancreatic enzymes for malabsorption, nutritional support

rows.label: Complications
items: VTE, biliary infection, gastric outlet obstruction, exocrine insufficiency, diabetes
Resection → pancreatic fistula, delayed gastric emptying, malabsorption

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation; no average-risk population screening; selected hereditary high-risk patients → MRI/EUS surveillance

rows.label: Mimics
items: Choledocholithiasis: colicky pain, ductal stone
Autoimmune pancreatitis: IgG4 elevation, diffuse pancreatic enlargement
Chronic pancreatitis: calcification, recurrent pain, prior inflammation

table.title: Functional neuroendocrine tumors
rows: ↑Insulin/C-peptide during supervised fast; negative sulfonylurea screen

pancreatic-cancer.evidence: Not checked online; established pancreatic oncology teaching.

pancreatitis.name: Pancreatitis
pancreatitis.scope: Acute pancreatitis, chronic pancreatitis, exocrine and endocrine insufficiency
pancreatitis.core: Epigastric pain radiating to the back with pancreatic inflammation may be acute; repeated injury produces irreversible chronic insufficiency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Gallstones, alcohol, triglycerides >1,000 mg/dL, ERCP, hypercalcemia, medications
Chronic: prolonged alcohol/tobacco exposure, genetic disease, duct obstruction, autoimmune disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Severe constant pain, vomiting, tenderness, ileus; chronic disease adds steatorrhea and weight loss
★ **Hypoxemia, hypotension, oliguria, persistent SIRS** → early monitored/ICU assessment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Premature intrapancreatic enzyme activation → autodigestion and systemic inflammation
Chronic fibrosis destroys acinar/islet tissue; lipase may normalize despite advanced disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Acute diagnosis: **2 of 3**—typical pain, lipase ≥3× ULN, characteristic imaging
RUQ ultrasound evaluates gallstones; triglycerides, calcium, liver tests identify cause
Contrast CT for uncertain diagnosis, deterioration, or failure to improve after 48–72 hours; not routine immediately
Chronic: CT/MRCP shows calcification/duct changes; fecal elastase <200 supports exocrine insufficiency

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute: **moderate lactated Ringer resuscitation**, frequent reassessment, analgesia, electrolyte correction; avoid overload
★ **Early oral low-fat feeding** within 24–48 hours if tolerated; enteral tube feeding if unable
Biliary with cholangitis → urgent ERCP; mild gallstone disease → cholecystectomy before discharge
Sterile necrosis: no antibiotics; infected: penetrating antibiotics, delayed step-up drainage/debridement
Chronic: stop alcohol/tobacco; pancreatic enzymes, nutrition/fat-soluble vitamins, pain and diabetes management

rows.label: Complications
items: ARDS, AKI, shock, hypocalcemia; local necrosis, vascular thrombosis, hemorrhage
Pseudocyst after >4 weeks; infected collection, obstruction; chronic disease → pancreatic cancer and brittle diabetes

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Treat cause**: gallbladder removal, triglyceride control, avoid culprit drug and alcohol
Post-ERCP rectal indomethacin in eligible patients; selected pancreatic duct stenting

rows.label: Mimics
items: Perforated ulcer: rigid abdomen/free air
Mesenteric ischemia: pain-exam mismatch; MI: ischemic ECG/troponin pattern

table.title: Severity and collections
rows: Transient dysfunction ≤48 hours or local complication

pediatric-exanthems.name: Pediatric exanthems
pediatric-exanthems.scope: Measles (rubeola), rubella (German measles), roseola infantum (HHV-6), erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19 fifth disease), scarlet fever, varicella, clinical appearance, complications
pediatric-exanthems.core: Fever with a childhood rash: use fever timing, rash progression, mucosal findings, immunization status, and pregnancy exposure to distinguish causes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Incomplete immunization, daycare/school exposure, travel; immunosuppression increases severe viral disease
Pregnant contacts require prompt assessment after rubella, parvovirus, or varicella exposure

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Toxic appearance**, petechiae/purpura, hypotension, meningismus → evaluate invasive infection immediately
Measles: cough, coryza, conjunctivitis precede rash; rubella: posterior auricular/suboccipital adenopathy
Varicella: trunk/scalp predominance; oral mucosal lesions may accompany the skin eruption

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Parvovirus suppresses erythroid precursors; congenital infection can cause severe fetal anemia
VZV remains latent in sensory ganglia; HHV-6 commonly causes febrile illness in infants

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected measles → **airborne isolation**, notify public health; respiratory PCR plus serum IgM
Scarlet fever → rapid GAS test; negative pediatric test → throat culture
Typical roseola/fifth disease: clinical; atypical vesicles → VZV PCR; rubella → public-health serology/PCR

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Scarlet fever → **penicillin or amoxicillin**; other uncomplicated exanthems generally supportive
Measles → hydration, complication care, clinician-supervised vitamin A for children
Severe/immunocompromised varicella → **IV acyclovir**; avoid aspirin in children

rows.label: Complications
items: Measles: pneumonia, encephalitis, delayed SSPE; rubella: congenital cataracts, deafness, PDA
Parvovirus: aplastic crisis, hydrops; roseola: febrile seizures
Varicella: bacterial superinfection, pneumonia, cerebellitis; GAS: rheumatic fever, glomerulonephritis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **MMR and varicella vaccines**; live vaccines contraindicated during pregnancy and severe immunosuppression
Measles exposure: MMR within 72 hours or immune globulin within 6 days for eligible contacts

rows.label: Mimics
items: Kawasaki disease: ≥5 days fever, conjunctivitis, oral/extremity changes
Drug eruption: medication exposure without characteristic infectious sequence

table.title: Signature rash
rows: Koplik spots; face → downward confluent rash
Sandpaper rash, Pastia lines, strawberry tongue

pericardial-disease.name: Pericardial disease
pericardial-disease.scope: Acute pericarditis, pericardial effusion, tamponade, constrictive pericarditis
pericardial-disease.core: Pericardial inflammation, fluid accumulation, or fibrosis produces distinct chest-pain and impaired-filling syndromes; hemodynamic effect depends on accumulation rate.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Viral/idiopathic, autoimmune disease, uremia, malignancy, TB, radiation, cardiac surgery
Early post-MI inflammation or delayed immune-mediated Dressler syndrome; trauma/anticoagulation can cause hemopericardium

rows.label: Clues
items: Pericarditis: sharp pleuritic positional pain, better leaning forward; friction rub may be transient
★ Tamponade: **hypotension, elevated JVP, muffled sounds**, pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg; triad often incomplete
Constrictive disease: edema/ascites, Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock, prominent y descent

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inflamed surfaces cause pain; fluid or scar limits diastolic filling and stroke volume
Tamponade equalizes diastolic pressures; constriction exaggerates ventricular interdependence with respiration

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Pericarditis: ≥2 of **typical pain, rub, diffuse ST elevation/PR depression, new effusion**
Troponin elevation suggests myocardial involvement; CRP supports inflammation; echo assesses fluid and ventricular function
★ **Urgent bedside echo** for suspected tamponade: right-sided chamber collapse, plethoric IVC
Constrictive suspicion → echo, CT/MRI for thickening/calcification; catheterization if diagnosis remains uncertain

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Tamponade → **urgent pericardiocentesis**; IV fluids bridge; avoid diuresis/positive-pressure ventilation
Purulent/traumatic effusion or recurrent difficult drainage → surgical drainage/window; antibiotics for bacterial cause
Stable effusion → treat cause, serial echo; low voltage alone never determines drainage
High-risk features → admit: fever, large effusion, immunosuppression, anticoagulation, subacute onset, NSAID failure

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent inflammation, arrhythmia/myocarditis, obstructive shock; procedural drainage → cardiac injury
Rapid decompression can rarely cause ventricular dysfunction; NSAIDs → GI/renal injury, colchicine → diarrhea

rows.label: Prevention
items: Colchicine course: first episode 3 months; recurrence ≥6 months; taper anti-inflammatory drugs after remission
Exercise restriction until clinical/inflammatory resolution; optimize dialysis for uremic disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: STEMI: regional ST elevation with reciprocal changes; urgent coronary evaluation if uncertain
Restrictive cardiomyopathy: myocardial disease, less respiratory ventricular discordance
PE: thrombotic risk, acute RV strain

table.title: Nonemergency definitive management
rows: Ibuprofen + colchicine; aspirin preferred after MI
Selected low-dose glucocorticoid or IL-1 blockade

peripheral-artery-disease.name: Peripheral artery disease
peripheral-artery-disease.scope: Claudication, aortoiliac (Leriche) disease, critical and acute limb ischemia
peripheral-artery-disease.core: Atherosclerotic limb hypoperfusion ranges from exertional claudication to rest pain, tissue loss, or abrupt limb-threatening arterial occlusion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, diabetes, age, CKD, hypertension, dyslipidemia; coronary/cerebrovascular atherosclerosis commonly coexists
AF, aneurysm, graft disease, hypercoagulability predispose acute occlusion

rows.label: Clues
items: Diminished pulses, cool shiny skin, hair loss, dependent rubor, distal nonhealing ulcers
★ **Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia** → acute limb ischemia
Sensory/motor deficits signal threatened limb; do not await all six findings

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fixed arterial narrowing limits exercise perfusion; progressive failure reduces resting tissue oxygenation
Acute embolus/thrombus prevents collateral compensation, rapidly injuring nerves and muscle

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ABI ≤0.90** confirms PAD; 0.91–0.99 borderline; >1.40 suggests noncompressible arteries
Exertional symptoms with normal resting ABI → exercise ABI; noncompressible vessels → toe-brachial index
Duplex, CTA/MRA define anatomy when revascularization planned; urgent Doppler exam in acute ischemia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic PAD: **clopidogrel or aspirin + high-intensity statin**, smoking cessation, structured exercise
Cilostazol improves claudication; contraindicated in any heart failure
